en: The *Tushita Guijing Ji* (Collection on the Mirror of Tuṣita) explains the origins and the reasons for its composition. Initially, the attendant of the Original Teacher, the Elder Yuemu, entered the Way in his youth;

through diligent cultivation and secret practice, he attained signs of rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven. Among both the monastic and the lay, there were none who did not feel moved by admiration and inquiry.

Alas! At that time, the scholar Zengtong Shao addressed the Master, saying: "I have heard, Master, that there exists a 'Collection on Rebirth in the West' (Xifang wangsheng ji) currently in circulation.

Yet, as for rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven, there have been many renowned sages throughout both ancient and modern times; why is it that there is none [for this] alone? I pray that you, Master, will compose such a work."

"May this serve as a mirror for ten thousand generations. The Master said, "Excellent! Your question is truly a fine medicine for curing illness and a compassionate boat for crossing the sea of suffering.
It is because ordinary beings, in a single thought, lose touch with the truth and falsely cling to the shadows of sensory objects that they drift through birth and death, with no hope of return.
They sink and rise among the six realms of existence; how can they escape the three worlds? Without yet attaining the stage of the Three Worthies or the Ten Sages..."

O Sage, how could one possibly escape the realm of birth through segmented existence? How much more so in this degenerate age, where the arrogant and deluded mostly mistake the shadows of the conscious mind for the realization of nature and the awakening to the Way;
they erroneously take the flash of a spark or a bolt of lightning to be the final resolution of birth and death.

They indulge in empty talk at will, repudiating cause and effect, and they revile those who uphold the precepts as being attached to forms, while disparaging those who study the teachings as merely poring over old paper. They deprecate the past...

Those who are born with such small roots and inferior ignorance do not contemplate the aspirations of Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna to behold Amitābha, nor the vows of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu to see Maitreya.
What kind of roots and what kind of ignorance are theirs, that they would recklessly disparage the sages and saints, and lightly slander the sūtras and the vinaya?

Who will take one’s place for the retribution of sin? Though one may speak of sudden enlightenment, habitual delusions have not yet been eliminated. Once one enters another’s belly, the darkness that veils the transition between lives is unavoidable.
Wuzu Jie, Qingcaotang, Elder Xun, and Head Seat Yan serve as sufficient precedents. When consciousness and perceptions fly about in confusion, one may attempt to equal the ancient sages;

when afflictions burn like a blazing fire, one may claim to transcend the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Yet without realizing the birthlessness of phenomena, one will ultimately follow [the cycle of rebirth].
The consciousness of karma flows on; yet one abandons Amitābha and Maitreya—the true Great Spiritual Friends—and fails to take them as objects of contemplation.

Guanyin and Shizhi, as well as Tiantai and Jingci, are truly excellent companions; why not draw near to them? Juesheng’s mother, Lady Zou, has already received the compassionate guidance of the World-Honored One and attained rebirth in the Inner Court.
This profound grace is vast and boundless, and she finds no way to repay it. She therefore again entreats her original [spiritual guide].
"Master, quickly complete this compilation so that it may serve as a precious raft for the fourfold assembly and as sustenance for future generations.

Thereupon, the Master examined various sūtras, śāstras, and biographical records, as well as all that he had seen and heard, compiling them into a volume. He entrusted me with carving it into printing blocks to disseminate it throughout the world.
Jueyin then asked the Master, "I wonder, does your aspiration lie in the Western Pure Land, or in Tuṣita? The Master replied:
The monk said, "I may ask you to remove the wooden peg. The Master said, "I do not understand the sound of 'wooden peg' (moku-ketsu). The monk exclaimed, "Heaven! Heaven!
The Master said, "I beg the Venerable One to show me compassion and explain this. The Master replied, "My tongue is not functioning well today;
wait for another time and I will tell you. Jueyin bowed and recounted the entire sequence of events. (Wuzu Ji’s later incarnation was Su Dongpo; Qingcaotang’s later incarnation was Zeng Gongliang.)
Lord Lu was the later incarnation of Elder Xun; Minister Li was the later incarnation of Head Seat Yan; and Qin Gui, the son of the Qin family, was the later incarnation of the monk from Yandang.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Baoxiang Forest in Nanhai, Guangzhou, at Qizhou.
Volume One: All Earth-Bodhisattvas who manifest traces through transformation dwell in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they [employ] various colors...
Manifesting universally through all gates to guide and transform all sentient beings so that they may together return to the shore of enlightenment, the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Manas addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, this Maitreya Bodhisattva is in his final birth before succession (*ekajātipratibaddha*), next in line after the World-Honored One to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Has he attained this Śūraṅgama Samādhi? The Buddha—

He said: "All those bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages, who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), and who have received the true position of a Buddha—all have attained this Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately manifested his supernatural power, such that the entire assembly saw within all the Jambudvīpas of this trichiliocosm nothing but Maitreya Bodhisattva; or they saw—
Sometimes they see them in the heavens; sometimes they see them among humans; sometimes they see them as renunciants; sometimes they see them as householders;
sometimes they see them serving the Buddha like Ānanda; sometimes they see them with wisdom like Śāriputra; sometimes they see them with supernatural powers like Maudgalyāyana;
sometimes they see them practicing *dhūta* austerities like Mahākāśyapa; sometimes they see them preaching the Dharma like Pūrṇa; or sometimes they see them in secret conduct like...
Rāhula, some saw him upholding the Vinaya like Upāli; some saw his divine eye like Aniruddha; some saw him practicing dhyāna like Revata.
In all such instances, they saw Maitreya. Some saw him entering various cities, towns, and villages to beg for food;
some saw him preaching the Dharma; and some saw him sitting in meditation. At that time, the bodhisattvas and...
The celestial hosts all beheld the supernatural power and majesty of Maitreya Bodhisattva as he manifested the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

Having seen this, they were filled with great joy and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is like pure gold which, though repeatedly forged and polished, does not lose its essential nature.
These Great Beings are likewise; wherever they are tested, they are able to manifest [their true nature] without fail."
The inconceivable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). If one can penetrate this samādhi, it should be known that one will then be able to penetrate all the practices of the paths of the three vehicles.
The rest is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, regarding what the youth Sudhana saw upon entering the Vairocana Pavilion.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Sudhana: "I shall transform and deliver those who practiced the various deeds together with me in the past; now..."
At that time, those who had fallen away from the bodhicitta were also born in this Jambudvīpa realm,
in the kingdom of Mālava, in the village of Koṭa, into a brahmin family, in order to teach and transform their parents, relatives, and all the brahmins.
I dwell within this great celestial palace for the sake of conforming to the minds of sentient beings; for the sake of maturing the devaputras who share my practice in Tuṣita Heaven;
desiring to manifest the Dharma-gate of Great Wisdom at the time of my impending descent into birth;
and in order to engage in discourse with bodhisattvas in their final birth; and desiring to instruct those sent by Śākyamuni Tathāgata, so as to...
They were all fully awakened. Consequently, they passed away from this life and were reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. The *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* states:
The Buddha told Upāli, "The Tuṣita Heaven is a place of superior, virtuous, and wondrous merit, where the retribution for the ten wholesome deeds is realized.

Even if I were to remain in the world for one small kalpa and extensively explain the retribution of Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*) and the fruits of the ten wholesome deeds, I could not exhaustively describe them."
[End. (The two contemplations regarding the primary and secondary [recompense] are detailed as in the sutra text. Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, when did this Great Being pass away from Jambudvīpa and take birth in that heaven? The Buddha told Upāli:
"Twelve years ago, on the fifteenth day of the second month, in the village of Kappila in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, he was born into the family of the great Brahmin Pāpali."
In his original place of birth, he sat cross-legged as if entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

His body was the color of purple-gold, its radiance brilliant and dazzling like a hundred thousand suns, extending upward as far as the Tuṣita Heaven. His bodily relics were like cast golden images, neither moving nor shaking.
Within the halo surrounding his body, the characters and meanings of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and the Prajñāpāramitā shone forth clearly.
Then, the devas and humans immediately erected a magnificent stupa made of various jewels to make offerings to the śarīra.
At that time, within a terrace of the seven treasures and upon a lion throne in a maṇi palace in Tuṣita Heaven, he was suddenly born by transformation upon a lotus flower, sitting cross-legged.
His body was the color of Jāmbūnada gold and sixteen yojanas in height. Thirty...
He was fully endowed with the two primary marks and the eighty secondary characteristics.

Upon his crown was a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), and his hair was the color of deep blue lapis lazuli. His celestial crown was adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of *śakrābhilagna* mani-jewels and *cintāmaṇi* gems.
Within that celestial crown were five hundred billion colors, and within each color were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of manifested Buddhas. These manifested...
The Bodhisattva served as his attendant. Furthermore, great bodhisattvas from other directions, possessing mastery over the eighteen transformations at will, resided within the celestial crown.

From the white tuft of hair between Maitreya’s eyebrows, a radiance issued forth, manifesting in the colors of a hundred jewels, even extending to magnificent clouds of eighty-four thousand rays of light. Together with the various devaputras, they each sat down.
Upon a flower-seat, during the six periods of day and night, he constantly preached the practice of the Dharma-wheel of the stage of non-retrogression.
Within a single period, he brought five hundred *koṭi* of devaputras to fulfillment, causing them not to regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, he constantly preached this wheel of non-retrogression day and night, delivering the various devaputras.
After fifty-six billion years according to the reckoning of Jambudvīpa, he then descended to be born in Jambudvīpa.
This is called the causes and conditions for Maitreya Bodhisattva’s passing away from Jambudvīpa and being reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.

(Jambudvīpa is newly translated as Jambūdvīpa. This Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousand worlds contains ten billion Jambudvīpas. Kāpila Village is the same as Koṭa Settlement. Śakrābhilagna means "Capable of Conquering.

Kiṃśuka means "Reddish Color. Tuṣita is newly translated as Tuṣita; it means "Contented with Joy," because the devas there mostly cultivate the samādhi of contented joy; it is also called "Knowing Contentment," because they know satisfaction regarding the five desires.)

Master Fu: The Master’s surname was Fu, his given name was Xi, and his courtesy name was Xuānfēng. He was a native of Yìwū County in Wùzhōu. His father’s name was Xuāncí, with the courtesy name Guǎng'ài;
his mother was of the Wáng clan. Their family had been farmers for generations. In the fourth year of the Jiànwǔ era of the Qi dynasty, the year of Dīngchū, on the eighth day of the fifth month—
Born on a day of the sun, he was upright, serene, pure, and harmonious, possessing no attachments. In his youth, he did not pursue formal studies; at times, he would fish with the villagers.
Whenever he caught a fish, he would always place them in a bamboo basket and sink it into deep water, praying: "May those who wish to leave go; may those who wish to stay remain."
The people of the time considered him a fool. In the eleventh year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, at the age of sixteen, he married a woman of the Liu clan named Miaoguang.
They had two sons: the first was named Pujian, and the second was named Pucheng. In the first year of the Putong era, he was twenty-four years old.
While he was staying at Jieting Pond, he encountered a Brahman monk named Sengtoutuo (Śrīghoṣa), who said to the Great Being, "In the past, you and I made a vow together before the Buddha Vipaśyin.
You are now enjoying the splendors of the Tuṣita Heaven; when will you return?
He then instructed him to look at his reflection in the water. Thereupon, [the Great Being] saw a halo and a jeweled canopy. The Great Being smiled and said, "The incense burner..."
"The bellows produce mostly dull iron; the gate of a skilled physician is always full of patients.
Since saving sentient beings is my urgent task, what leisure have I to contemplate the pleasures of heaven? Thereupon, he constructed a hermitage between two *śāla* trees at the foot of a mountain.
This is the present-day Shuanglin Temple. He styled himself the "Future Liberated Mahāsattva of Good Wisdom Beneath the Twin Trees," and daily attended to Miaoguang.
He practiced the Way at night and beheld the three Buddhas—Śākyamuni, Suvarṇapuṣpa, and Dīpaṃkara—emitting light that gathered into the body of a Mahāsattva.

From this body, a wondrous fragrance constantly issued forth. Furthermore, he was moved by the appearance of the seven Buddhas following one another, with Śākyamuni leading the way and Vimalakīrti following behind.
Every morning when the bell rang, an immortal would descend from the void to join him in rejoicing and practicing the Way. He once said to his disciples:
He said, "I have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. He also said, "I have attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

The disciples all said, "The Śūraṅgama Samādhi can only be attained by Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*). Therefore, it was known that this Great Being was a Bodhisattva dwelling in the tenth stage, merely manifesting his traces in common with ordinary people.
He addressed the great assembly, saying, "If one studies the Way and does not encounter a teacher of non-arising (*anutpāda*),"
"In the end, you would not have attained the Way. I am one who has realized non-arising in the present. Previously I concealed this matter;
now I shall no longer hide it, so as to show it to you. Furthermore, when the disciples prostrated themselves, the Great Being said to them:
"When you prostrate to me, you are merely prostrating to the Buddha within the hall; that is my own image. He further said: "In a dream, I recalled my former teacher, whose name was..."
He said: "Excellent, World-Honored One. Someone asked: "World-Honored One, is the teacher the one at the time of attaining the Way, or the one at the time of generating the aspiration?
He replied: "The teacher is not the one at the time of generating the aspiration. When that Buddha appeared in the world, I was a king and made offerings to him.
That Buddha’s lifespan was eighty thousand years; when I become a Buddha, my lifespan shall likewise be so. [This concludes] the sixth section of the Great Penetration.

In the [blank] year, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) visited the Imperial Palace. Emperor Wu asked the Great Being, "Whom do you take as your teacher? He replied, "I follow that from which there is nothing to follow;

I have no teacher to serve, and I attend to nothing to attend to. From this time forth, renowned monks gathered like clouds at this place, where the nectar of immortality (amṛta) constantly descended.
The Great Being personally transcribed over one thousand scrolls of the Sūtras and Vinaya, praying that all sentient beings might be freed from suffering and attain liberation.
The Great Being came to the capital three times; those he converted, both monastics and laypeople, were beyond counting.
He said to his disciples, "Among the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, I am but one Buddha. If you wish to be born among those thousand Buddhas, you shall immediately behold me.
He further addressed the assembly, saying, "When I cast off this body, I shall meet with Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa; I will go briefly to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and soon return to the Tuṣita Heaven."

"Lead the heavens! If you vow to be born there, you shall immediately behold me. In the eighth year of the Datong era, he established a vow to observe the highest fast (upavāsa), composing a prayer that read:
"I, the disciple Shanhui, now address Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One, and all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time."

Pervading all of empty space and throughout the entire Dharma-realm, I take refuge in the Three Jewels which abide eternally. This disciple reflects that in this present life there has been nothing to fulfill my heart’s desire in terms of giving alms to rescue and deliver suffering sentient beings.
From this day forth, I vow for three years to observe the supreme fast, abstaining from food and drink on the sixth day of every month.
Through the suffering of this hunger and thirst, I shall, on behalf of all sentient beings, repay their karmic offenses and swiftly [attain liberation].
Having attained liberation, he extensively practiced giving with food that required no cultivation, vowing that all sentient beings, in every lifetime,
may be fully provided with immeasurable wealth and Dharma, forever free from the defilement of craving, refrain from the three types of karma, attain great *dhāraṇī*, and subdue all māras.
Having attained the Unsurpassed Way, he vowed to sacrifice his body, life, and wealth, universally making offerings to all Buddhas for the sake of all beings.
He strictly observed the supreme fast of non-eating and entered *parinirvāṇa*. Holding firm to his resolve, he burned his own body as a great bright lamp to make offerings to the Triple Gem.
He then addressed the assembly, saying: "Do not harbor grief or distress. All things are subject to birth and death; all affairs reach completion."
There is decay. All the affections of the world must inevitably part. Now, casting off this defiled and turbid body, I shall attain the unsurpassed, pure Dharma-body.
I pray that you, my disciples, harbor no grief or longing; may we never be parted throughout birth after birth, remaining as kinsmen forever until the Way of Buddhahood is realized.
Let us simply lead one another and together prepare firewood at the Twin Trees.

Atop the mountain peak, they constructed fire shrines. They made this vow: "By virtue of these causes and conditions, may we surely perform the work of a Buddha in future worlds, universally delivering all beings so that we may together attain liberation.

On the eighth day of the fourth month, nineteen disciples—including Liu Jianyi and Fan Nanta—each requested to serve as proxies for their master, observing the supreme fast of non-eating and offering the sacrifice of self-immolation by fire.

They supported the Three Jewels. Furthermore, there were disciples from the four assemblies who pierced their hearts, burned their fingers, and cut off their ears, praying that the Mahāsattva would remain long in the world.
He also said, "I attained the Way forty kalpas ago, whereas the World-Honored One Śākyamuni has only recently resolved to attain it;
it is because he was able to renounce his body and practice asceticism that he became a Buddha before me. When Śrīgupta entered parinirvāṇa, the Mahāsattva...
He knew this within his own mind. He then assembled his disciples and said, "Master Sōng has already returned to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace to await me.
Those who were to be saved by me together with the sentient beings have all departed. I shall certainly not remain long in this world.

Thereupon, he composed the "Verses on Returning to the Source" in twelve stanzas. This was in the first year of the Taian era, the year of Jichou (529 CE), in the fourth month of summer, on the day of Bingshen.
On the first day of the month, the Great Being fell ill. He addressed his two sons, the Dharma Masters Pu-jian and Pu-cheng, saying:
"I have come from the Fourth Heaven for the sake of delivering sentient beings. You must carefully guard the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; diligently practice the six perfections;

and perform the rite of repentance so as to avoid falling into the three miserable realms. The two masters then asked: "If you do not remain in this world, the assembly may become scattered. What shall become of the Buddha hall?"
"How can this not be accomplished? The Great Being said, "After my passing from this world, it may manifest signs.

On the twenty-fourth day, the day of Yimao (the second day of the Earth-Hare branch), the Great Being entered *nirvāṇa*. He was seventy-three years old at the time. His flesh did not change color for three days;

his entire body then became warm again, his features remained upright and pure, and his hands became supple when turned over. After another seven days, Chen Zhong, the Magistrate of Wushang County, arrived.
The Elder came seeking incense to establish a karmic connection. He took the incense and passed it through the fourfold assembly in succession until it reached the Great Being (Mahāsattva).

The Great Being still received the incense with his hands turned backward. The śramaṇas Fa-xuan and others said, "We are fortunate to have been granted the privilege of witnessing the Bodhisattva manifesting the sign of returning to the source.
That he personally transmitted the incense demonstrates that existence is not different from non-existence, so that future generations may know of this sacred transformation."
Regarding the remaining fragrance: before the Great Being passed away, he said to his disciples, "After my parinirvāṇa, do not move my bed.
Seven days hence, a venerable monk named Famen shall arrive bringing a woven image of Maitreya Buddha;
it shall remain permanently upon my bed to serve as a representation of my physical form. When the seven days arrived, he indeed brought the image of Maitreya Buddha along with...
A small bronze bell was placed upon the Great Being’s bed; when he was in a state of intense fervor, he prostrated himself and wept.

In a brief moment, it suddenly vanished (as recorded in detail in his biography; this was the manifestation of the Great Being’s realization of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, as clarified in the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*).
Upāli (Qichi) the Monk was from Fenghua County in Mingzhou. Known as the Cloth Bag Monk (Puduo), his clan and family name were unknown; he called himself Qichi.

His physical form was stout and portly, with a furrowed brow and a protruding belly. He had no fixed dwelling and slept wherever he happened to be. He constantly carried a cloth bag slung over a staff.
All the implements for his sustenance were stored within a single bag. When he entered markets, shops, or villages, he would beg for whatever he saw;
even if it were vinegar, sauce, fish, or pickles, he would cast them into his sack. At that time, he was called "The Man of the Long Embankment. He himself spoke this verse:
"One bowl of food from a thousand homes, A solitary body wandering ten thousand li. With azure eyes, I see few people; I ask the way at the head of white clouds. Or, amidst the snow...
While sleeping in the middle of the day, his body remained free of snow; everyone marveled at this. When he indicated good or bad fortune to others, signs and omens invariably manifested.

During periods of drought, he would drag about high-toothed wooden clogs, and people knew it would surely rain. During floods, he would tie on wet straw sandals, and people knew it would surely clear.
Sometimes he sat at street corners, or stood in the middle of the road, where children vied with one another to chase him, gathering in groups to play with the Master.
There is a verse that says: "Right and wrong, hatred and love—these prevail greatly in the world. Reflect upon this carefully: what can you do? Widen your belly and must endure insults;
Open your heart and let others be as they will. If you meet a kindred spirit, follow the proper measure;
Even if you encounter an enemy, remain in harmony. If you can resolve these matters of the mind, You will naturally realize the six pāramitās. I.
There is a cloth bag; empty space is without obstruction. When unfolded, it pervades the ten directions; when entering, it is Avalokiteśvara.
I have one Buddha-body that no person in the world recognizes. It is neither molded nor adorned; it is neither carved nor engraved.
There is not a single drop of plaster, nor a single speck of color. People cannot paint it, and thieves cannot steal it. Its substance—

The marks are fundamentally natural; they are pure and do not require wiping away. Although he was a single body, he manifested himself as thousands, tens of billions, and hundreds of millions of bodies.
In the third year of the Zhengming era of the Liang dynasty, the Master sat upright upon a flat rock on the eastern perimeter of Yuelin Temple and demonstrated his entry into *nirvāṇa*.

He spoke this verse: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; He manifests himself as thousands, tens of billions, and hundreds of millions of bodies. From time to time he appears to people of the age, Yet people of the age [do not recognize him] themselves."

He did not recognize [him]. When the verse was finished, he passed away peacefully. The assembly buried him together. Later, he was seen appearing in another province, likewise walking while carrying a cloth bag on his back.

The fourfold assembly vied with one another to paint his image. (The "thousand times ten million" refers to the three thousand great chiliocosms of the Sahā world; the "ten thousand times ten million" refers to the four great continents.)
In Central India, to the east of the Bodhi tree, there is a vihāra one hundred and sixty to seven hundred feet high.
Its foundation at the base is over twenty paces wide, constructed of blue bricks and plastered with lime. Each tiered niche contains a golden image, and the four walls—
It was carved with extraordinary designs: some in the shape of linked pearls, others as images of celestial immortals. Atop it were placed precious vases of gold and copper.
On its eastern side, a multi-storied pavilion was constructed, its eaves and roof rising in three tiers.

Its rafters, pillars, beams, doors, and windows were adorned with silver and gold carvings and embellished with inlaid pearls and jade. The inner chambers and deep halls featured three successive sets of interconnected doors.
On the left and right of the outer gate, there are each a niche chamber. On the left is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; on the right is an image of the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
They are cast from white silver and are over ten feet in height. This was the original site of the vihāra.
King Aśoka first constructed a small vihāra here, and later a Brahmin further expanded its construction. Initially, there was a Brahmin who did not believe in the Buddha.
The Brahmin was devoted to Maheśvara. Having heard that the deity resided within the Snowy Mountains (Himavat), he went there with his younger brother to offer prayers.
The deity said, "Regarding all requests for boons, they bear fruit only when one possesses merit; they are not granted by your prayers alone, nor can I fulfill them.
The Brahmin asked, "What merit must be cultivated so that one's heart's desire may be fulfilled? The deity replied, "If you wish to plant the seeds of goodness, seek the supreme..."
"The Field of Merit. The Bodhi tree is the place where the fruit of Buddhahood is realized. You ought to return at once;
go to the Bodhi tree, construct a great vihāra, dig a large pond, and perform various offerings. Your aspirations shall then be fulfilled.

Having received this divine mandate, the Brahmin conceived great faith and returned accompanied by his followers. The elder brother constructed the vihāra, and the younger brother dug the pond. Thereupon, [the works] were extensively...

He practiced offerings and diligently sought his heart's desires, which were all subsequently fulfilled. Serving as a minister to the king, he bestowed whatever stipends and rewards he received upon others in charity.
Once the vihāra was completed, he recruited artisans, intending to fashion an image of the Tathāgata as he first attained enlightenment;
however, time passed and no one responded to the call. After a long while, a brāhmaṇa came and addressed the assembly, saying: "I am skilled..."
He drew the wondrous marks of the Tathāgata. The assembly asked, "Now that we are about to create an image, what will be required? He replied, "Only fragrant clay.
"It should be placed within a vihāra and illuminated by a single lamp; once I have entered, the door must be firmly closed for six months. After six months had passed...

Then they were permitted to open the door. At that time, the assembly of monks all followed his instructions. With four months still remaining and six months not yet complete, the multitude was struck with wonder and opened [the door] to look inside.
They saw that within the vihāra, the Buddha image sat solemnly in the full lotus posture.
The right foot is placed above; the left hand is drawn in, while the right hand hangs down. He sits facing east, with a solemn air as if truly present.
The seat is four chi and two cun high and one zhang, two chi and five cun wide. The image is one zhang, one chi and five cun tall;

the distance between the two knees is eight chi and eight cun, and the distance between the two shoulders is six chi and two cun. His marks and signs are complete, and his compassionate countenance appears as if real. Contemplate this.
On the right breast, while the application of the polish was not yet complete, no person was seen; thus it was verified that divine discernment had been exercised.

The assembly all sighed with sorrow and earnestly requested to know [the reason]. There was a śramaṇa whose long-held mind was pure and sincere; he was moved to have a dream in which he saw the former brahmin, who told him: "I am the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
Fearing that the artisan’s thoughts might fail to fathom the holy countenance, I have come in person."
Regarding the depiction of the Buddha’s image where his right hand hangs downward: long ago, when the Tathāgata was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the celestial Māra came to harass him.
The Earth Goddess announced her arrival; one of her manifestations emerged first to assist the Buddha in subduing the Māra.

The Tathāgata said to her, "Do not be anxious or afraid; by the power of my patience, I shall surely subdue him. The King of Māras asked, "Who will serve as a witness to this? Thereupon, the Tathāgata lowered [his hand].
He pointed to the ground, saying, "There is evidence here. At that time, a goddess of the second earth-level leaped forth to bear witness.
Therefore, the hand of the image today is modeled after its ancient downward gesture. When the multitude realized this divine manifestation, there was none who was not moved by grief.

Thereupon, before the milk had even finished flowing, he filled the site with various jewels, pearl necklaces, and precious crowns, adorned with rare treasures. King Śreṇika did not believe in the Triple Gem; he launched an attack—
Having reached the Bodhi tree, he intended to destroy this image. However, upon beholding its compassionate countenance, his heart could not endure it.
He turned his carriage back to return home and commanded his chief minister, saying: "You must remove this Buddhist statue and install an image of Maheśvara.

The minister received the decree; trembling with fear, he sighed and said: "To destroy a Buddhist image would bring calamity for kalpas; yet to disobey the King’s command would lead to the loss of my life and the extinction of my clan. He then...
When he had retreated in this manner, what was the appropriate course of action? He summoned those with faith to be employed as laborers and, before the image, laid bricks crosswise to form a wall.
Feeling ashamed by the resulting darkness, he further placed bright lamps before the brick wall and painted a figure of Maheśvara.
When the work was completed and the report sent back, the King heard it and was struck with fear; blisters broke out over his entire body, and his skin was torn and lacerated. Not long after, he...
The image was lost and destroyed. The chief minister galloped back and demolished the enclosing walls. Although many days had passed, the lamps and their contents had not extinguished;

the image remains to this day, its divine power undiminished. (King Aśoka is the one referred to here as "Wúyōu Wáng. The term *brāhmaṇa* is translated here as "Fànzhì," which is one of the four castes of India.)
I heard that in the country of Koṅkanapura in South India, within a great monastery beside the palace city, there is a vihāra over fifty feet high.
Inside it is a carved sandalwood image of Maitreya Bodhisattva, over ten feet in height. Or... [it reaches...]
On days of fasting, a divine light shines forth; this was constructed by the Arhat Śrutaviṃśati-koti.

Venerable Madhyāntika (the disciple of Venerable Kuvula) traveled from the city of Maṅgala in North India, crossing mountains and valleys and traveling upstream along the Indus River. On his journey...
It was perilous. The mountain valleys were deep and dark; at times they traversed ropes, at other times they were dragged by iron chains.

The plank paths hung precariously over the void, and flying bridges were constructed in great danger. Climbing wooden ladders and treading upon stone steps, they traveled more than a thousand *li* until they reached the Dārilā Valley, which is the ancient capital of the kingdom of Udyāna.
This region produces much gold and saffron. Beside a great monastery in the middle of the Dārilā Valley...
There is a carved wooden image of Maitreya Bodhisattva, its golden hue radiant and brilliant, its spiritual perception subtly penetrating.
It stands over one hundred feet high and was fashioned by the Arhat Madhyāntika (formerly called Madhyāntika, which is an error). By means of his supernormal powers, the Arhat...
He led artisans up to Tuṣita Heaven to personally behold the wondrous marks; after three such visits, the work was finally completed.
Since the arrival of this image, the Dharma has flowed eastward. Furthermore, to the northwest of the great city of the kingdom of Yodheya in Central India...
Within the monastery is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. Inside it is one *śeṣa* (one *lǐng*) of the Tathāgata’s relics.
Formerly, at this very spot, the World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma for seven days for the sake of the multitudes of devas and humans.
Beside it are the sites of the seats and the walking paths of the three past Buddhas. Adjacent to this is...

There is a statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva; although its physical dimensions are small, its majestic spirit is imposing. Its spiritual discernment communicates in secret, and miraculous events arise from time to time.
King Yingzheng...
In Central India, more than three hundred *li* to the southwest of the kingdom of Kośala, one reaches Mount Kṛṣṇagiri.
It rises prominently and loftily; its peaks and cliffs are steep and perilous. Lacking any precipices or valleys, it is as if composed of a single solid rock.

King Śrīmegha excavated this mountain for the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and established a monastery there. About ten or so *li* from the mountain, he also excavated a tunnel that passes directly through the center of the mountain.
Below, they hollowed out and carved away the rock. Within it were long corridors and overhanging eaves, as well as lofty terraces and multi-storied pavilions.

The pavilions had five stories, and each story contained four courtyards, all of which housed *vihāras*. In each, golden images were cast, equal in size to the body of the Buddha, their exquisite craftsmanship reaching the pinnacle of artistic ingenuity.

As for the remaining decorations, they were adorned solely with gold and jewels. From the high peaks of the mountain, flying springs cascaded down, flowing around the multi-storied pavilions and interlacing through the corridors and verandas.
The windows were open to the outside, allowing light to illuminate the interior chambers.

When King Prasenajit first commissioned the construction of this monastery, the labor force was exhausted and the treasury was empty; before the work was even half-finished, his mind was filled with great sorrow and distress. Nāgārjuna said:

He said, "Great King, for what reason do you have such a look of sorrow? The King replied, "I have set forth a great resolve and dared to plant seeds of supreme merit, hoping they would remain eternally firm until the arrival of Maitreya.
Yet, before my achievements are complete, my resources are already exhausted. I harbor this regret constantly, sitting and waiting for the break of dawn. Nāgārjuna said, "Do not grieve.
The benefits of honoring merit and performing sublime good are inexhaustible. Since you possess such a vast vow,"
Without freedom from sorrow, there can be no salvation. Today we return to the palace; you shall experience the utmost joy.

When we go out on excursion again later to traverse the mountains and wilds, we shall arrive here once more to deliberate upon the construction of the monastery. Once the King had received this instruction, the great stones all transformed into gold.

As the King traveled and saw the gold, he rejoiced in his heart and mouth. Turning his carriage back to the place where Nāgārjuna resided, he said: "On this day’s hunt, [the site] was blessed by gods and spirits..."

The deluded ones saw what appeared to be heaps of gold within the mountain forests. Nāgārjuna said, "This is not a demonic delusion; it is because of the power of your utmost sincerity that this gold has appeared.
You should take and use it at once to accomplish your supreme undertaking. He then used it for the construction. When the work was finished, there was still a surplus.
Thereupon, within each of the five tiers, four great golden images were cast; the remaining materials were still piled in abundance, filling the various treasuries.
A thousand monks were gathered to reside therein for ritual recitations. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna [established] the teachings and Dharma proclaimed by Śākyamuni Buddha.

Furthermore, the treatises expounded by the various bodhisattvas were collected and categorized, and stored therein; thus, in the uppermost first layer, only Buddha images and various sūtras and śāstras were placed.
In the lowest fifth layer resided the lay attendants (*śrāmaṇera*) and their assets and utensils.
The three middle layers served as the dwellings for the monastic community. According to the accounts of former masters, once the construction of the Yǐngzhèng Monastery was completed:

Calculating the price of the salt consumed by the laborers, it amounted to nine koṭis of gold coins (Nāgārjuna—formerly translated as Longshu; *koṭi* means "one hundred billion" in the language of Tang).
Uttara (translated into Chinese as "Upper") was located in South India, in the kingdom of Cūḷika.
Not far to the west of the capital city, there was an old monastery, the site where the Bodhisattva Deva debated with an arhat.
Initially, the Bodhisattva Deva heard that this monastery contained an Uttara...
An Arhat who had attained the six supernormal powers and was endowed with the eight liberations eventually traveled from afar to seek him out, wishing to observe his exemplary conduct.
Upon arriving at the monastery, he sought lodging with the Arhat. In the place where the Arhat resided, there was only a single bed;
as Deva had no mat to sit upon, the Arhat gathered fallen leaves and bade him take his seat. The Arhat entered meditative absorption and did not emerge until the middle of the night. Deva...

At that time, Vasubandhu set forth his doubts and requested the Arhat to resolve them. As the Arhat explained each point according to the difficulty, Saṃghabhadra immediately followed up on the words with further inquiries.
When he reached the seventh turn of questioning, the Arhat remained silent and could not provide an answer. Secretly employing his supernormal powers, he went to Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya.
Maitreya provided the explanation and then said to him: "That Saṃghabhadra has practiced for kalpas upon kalpas; he is one of the [great] ones of the Bhadrakalpa."
[He was] among them. He shall succeed to the Buddha’s position; this is not something you can know. You should pay him deep reverence.

In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, he returned to his original seat and once again expounded the sublime meaning and analyzed the subtle words. Deva said to him, "This is the explanation of the noble wisdom of Maitreya Bodhisattva;
how could it be something that a worthy one such as yourself could thoroughly investigate? The Arhat replied, "Indeed, it is truly as you say."
The Master [Xuanzang] said, "This is the essence. Thereupon, he rose from his seat to pay his respects and offer thanks, deeply expressing his reverence and admiration.

To the south of the capital city of the country of Mahāratna in South India, not far away, there is a great mountain cliff where the Master of Śāstras, Bhāviveka, resided. The Master of Śāstras Bhāviveka...
The Master resided in the palace of the Asuras, awaiting the place where Maitreya Bodhisattva would attain Buddhahood.

The master’s noble character was vast and far-reaching, and his supreme virtue was profound and deep. Outwardly, he donned the robes of the Saṃgha; inwardly, he propagated the teachings of Nāgārjuna. In quiet contemplation, he thought:
"If it were not for Maitreya attaining Buddhahood, who could resolve my doubts? Before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, he recited...
Regarding the *Anusṛtacitta-dhāraṇī*, [the master] abstained from grains and subsisted only on water for three years.
Then, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara manifested a body of wondrous color and said to the Śāstrin, "What is your aspiration? He replied, "I wish to preserve this body until I may behold Maitreya.
Avalokiteśvara said, "Human life is precarious and fragile; the world is floating and illusory. You should cultivate supreme goodness and make your vow."
"If you are born in Tuṣita Heaven and pay your respects there, you will still see him quickly. The Master of Śāstras said, "One's resolve must not be diverted, and one's mind must not be divided.
The Bodhisattva said, "If that is so, you should go to Mount Gandhamādana in the kingdom of Mahānada.

To the south of the city, at the site where the Vajrapāṇi deity dwells among the mountain crags, those who recite the Vajrapāṇi mantra with utmost sincerity shall have this vow fulfilled. Thus it was said in the treatise.
The Master then went there and recited [the scriptures]. After three years, the deity spoke to him, saying, "What is your aspiration that you exert yourself so diligently?
The Master replied, "I wish to remain in this body until I may behold Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva pointed me here and sent me to request this;
will it not be up to you, O deity, to fulfill my vow? Thereupon, the deity bestowed upon him a secret formula and said to him:
"Within this rock lies the palace of an asura. If you invoke it according to the Dharma, the stone wall shall open; once it has opened, enter within and wait to see him.

The master of the treatises said, "I dwell in seclusion and have never seen such a thing; how could I know when a Buddha would appear? The deity replied, "When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you.
Having received these instructions, the master devoted himself single-mindedly to recitation and retention. Another three years passed, yet he had not yet [seen him].
With a different thought, he enchanted some mustard seeds and struck them against the stone wall; it opened wide and became a hollow passage.

At that time, a multitude of hundreds of thousands watched in wonder, forgetting to leave. The Master of Treatises stepped across the threshold and addressed the crowd, saying, "I have long prayed and waited to behold Maitreya."
Through the protective blessing of the Holy Spirit, his great vow was fulfilled. He should enter here to behold the Buddha’s manifestation together with us.
Those who heard this were terrified and none dared to step upon the threshold, deeming it a den of venomous serpents and fearing for their lives.

Despite repeated exhortations, only six people followed him inside. As the master of the treatises looked back and took his leave, the assembly entered at their leisure. Once they had entered, the stone wall—

They returned to their original state. The assembly was filled with awe and sighed in lamentation, regretting the error of their previous words. (Asura; formerly translated as Asura; here it means "Non-God.")
The Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra—Buddhabhadra means "Awakened Virtue" (Jiexian) in this language—was originally surnamed Śākya and was a native of Kapilavastu.

He was a descendant of King Amṛtodana. He was extensively learned in the various scriptures and attained mastery in many fields; from his youth, he was renowned for his expertise in meditation and the Vinaya.
He was constantly traveling with his fellow student Saṃghadatta through the kingdom of Kaśmīra, staying together for many years.

Although Saṃghadatta admired his brilliance and wisdom, he had not yet fathomed the man’s true nature. Later, while sitting in meditation in a closed room with the door shut, he suddenly saw Buddhabhadra appear.
Startled, he asked where he had come from. Buddhabhadra replied, "I have briefly gone to Tuṣita to pay my respects to Maitreya. Having spoken, he vanished instantly.

Dharmatāta knew him to be a sage, yet he had not fathomed the depth of his realization. Later, having repeatedly witnessed the holy man’s supernatural transformations, he prayed to him with a reverent heart and inquired;
only then did he learn that [the master] had attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
The Master of Śāstras Guṇaprabha was from the kingdom of Mathurā in Central India. From his youth, he was brilliant and outstanding; as he grew older, he became expansive and sagacious.

He was widely learned, possessed a powerful memory, and was a scholar of vast knowledge and extensive erudition. Originally, he practiced the Mahāyāna, yet had not yet fathomed its profound mysteries. Consequently, upon reading the *Vibhāṣā*...
Sa retreated from his [Mahāyāna] practice and studied the Hīnayāna, composing several dozen treatises that subverted the fundamental principles of the Mahāyāna.

He also produced over several dozen secular works to disparage and denounce his predecessors. Although he applied himself with profound thought to the Buddhist scriptures for many years, he could not resolve more than ten or so points;
despite his long period of diligent study, his doubts remained unresolved. At that time, there was an Arhat named Tianjun (Devasena) who traveled between Tuṣita Heaven and the human realm.
"Deva, Devaruci wishes to see Maitreya to resolve his doubts and seek further instruction. Deva-sena, by means of his supernatural powers, transported him to the celestial palace.
Having seen Maitreya, Devaruci merely bowed from afar and did not prostrate. Deva-sena said to him: 'Maitreya Bodhisattva is next in line to succeed to the Buddha’s position;
why are you so self-important as to dare not pay your respects? As you are about to receive his teachings, why do you not bow? Devaruci replied:"
He said, "Venerable sir, these words of yours are indeed a true instruction. However, I am a renunciant disciple;
Maitreya Bodhisattva enjoys celestial bliss and is not a fellow in the life of renunciation. To wish to pay him homage seems inappropriate.
Knowing that his pride was firm and that he was not a vessel for hearing the Dharma, [Maitreya] came and went three times, yet the disciple could not resolve his doubts. He then requested Deva-sena."

He wished once more to pay his respects, but the celestial army loathed his arrogance and treated him with contempt, refusing to respond. Since his desire was not fulfilled, De-guang (Guṇaprabha) gave rise to resentment;

he then proceeded to the Pūrva-vana (Eastern Forest) to cultivate and develop the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna-samādhi*). However, because his pride had not yet been eliminated, he did not realize the fruit at that time.
Dharma Master Daofa’s family name was Cao;
he was a native of Dunhuang. Having renounced his home to enter the Way, he specialized in the practice of Chan meditation. He also occasionally performed divine incantations.
Later, while traveling to Chengdu, he was invited by Wang Xiuzhi and Fei Kengzhi to serve as the presiding masters of Xingle and Xiangji Monasteries, where he instructed the assembly.

There was a practitioner who constantly practiced alms-seeking (*piṇḍapāta*), refusing special invitations or meals provided by the *saṃgha*. Whatever he obtained through begging, he would always set aside a portion to give to insects and birds.
Every evening, he would strip off his clothes and sit in the open air to feed the mosquitoes and gadflies; he continued in this manner for many years.

Later, while entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he saw Maitreya emit light from his navel, which illuminated the suffering retributions of the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*). Thereupon, he deepened his practice.

He was earnest and diligent, constantly sitting and never lying down. In the second year of the Yuanhui era, he passed away while in meditative absorption, sitting upright on his rope-cot with an appearance as if he were his usual self.
(Fenwei refers to begging for food.)
Chan Master Huilan’s surname was Cheng, and he was a native of Jiuquan. He once traveled to the Western Regions, where he carried a Buddha’s alms bowl upon his head.

Furthermore, in Kaśmīra, he studied the essentials of dhyāna under the bhikṣu Dharmatrāta. Dharmatrāta had previously entered meditative absorption and gone to Tuṣita Heaven to receive teachings from Maitreya.

Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts: he later bestowed the dharma of the precepts upon Lan. Upon returning to the kingdom of Jutián, he again transmitted the dharma of the precepts to the various monks of that region before returning to the eastern lands.
Emperor Wén of the Song dynasty invited him to reside at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhōng.

Emperor Xiào of the Wǔ dynasty established Zhōngxīng Temple and further issued an imperial decree that all meditation masters in the capital should follow his example and receive instruction from him.
Dharma Master Zhiyan was a native of Xiliangzhou.

He entered the monastic order in his early twenties and soon became renowned for his diligent application. Wearing patched robes and sitting in meditation, he maintained a vegetarian diet for the rest of his life.

Desiring to seek out the scriptures extensively, he traveled throughout the Western Regions, where he consulted and received instructions on the methods of dhyāna; his merit in this endeavor surpassed that of others.
Ten years later, he invited the Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra to return to the East to transmit the Dharma to this land.

In the fourth year of the Yuanjia era, together with the śramaṇa Baoyun, he translated the *Ratnolkā*, the *Vaipulya-prabhāsa-śuddha*, the *Saptabuddhaka*, and other sūtras. Previously, when Yan had not yet left the household life, he had received the five precepts;
however, he had committed minor transgressions against them. Later, upon entering the Way and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he constantly harbored doubts regarding this matter.
Having received the precepts, he was constantly filled with apprehension. Although he practiced meditative contemplation for many years, he could not achieve self-realization.

He subsequently traveled across the sea once more, returning to India to consult various learned and realized masters. There he encountered an Arhat bhikṣu, to whom he related his situation in detail.
The Arhat did not dare to provide a definitive judgment; instead, he entered a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and went to the Tuṣita Palace to consult Maitreya. Maitreya replied:
He attained the precepts. Yan Da was greatly delighted; thereupon he returned on foot. Upon reaching Jibin, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-eight.

During the third year of Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty, the monk Huashou was summoned by an imperial edict to attend an unrestricted great assembly (*anāvaraṇa-mahāpariṣad*). The Wei Emperor issued an edict inquiring about the monks and nuns of this land.
When asked about the origins of the precepts and what evidence there was for them, the various venerable ones were all unable to answer.

At that time, a bhikṣu requested to travel to the Western Regions to inquire of the sages regarding the origins of the precepts. Setting out from Chang’an, he arrived in India and encountered an arhat, to whom he addressed his question:
"Do the monks and nuns of China receive the precepts or not? The arhat replied: "I..."

"This is a minor sage; I do not know whether he will succeed or not. You remain here while I ascend to Tuṣita Heaven on your behalf to inquire of the World-Honored One Maitreya regarding whether or not he may come.
He shall then report back. Having spoken thus, he immediately entered meditative concentration and proceeded toward Tuṣita Heaven.

There he inquired in detail about the aforementioned matter. Maitreya replied, "Both monks and nuns shall receive the precepts. He then requested a formal verification, whereupon Maitreya took up gold...
Huayan said: "If the monks and nuns of the borderlands attain the precepts, I vow that these golden flowers shall enter the palms of the Arhats;
if they do not attain them, let them not enter. Having finished making this vow, he pressed the flowers against his hands, and the flowers entered his palms, appearing as a shadow one foot high.
Maitreya spoke, saying: "When you reach the bhikṣus in China, you should follow this same method as I have done here. The Arhat then descended.
As Maitreya spoke, he pressed a flower against the bhikṣu’s hand, and it immediately entered his palm, appearing as a manifestation one chi high.

Once this auspicious sign had been verified, at that time there were many monastics and laypeople from distant regions who came to admire and revere him; countless people sought to receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
He was thus named the Bhikṣu Huashou (Flower-Hand). When he was about to depart, there were eighteen people [who followed].
As for the others who aspired to dwell in the Western Regions, some perished from exposure to the winds and cold while venturing across the shifting sands.
Only the bhikṣu Huashou returned alone to the land of Han. On the day he originally departed, the deity Kapiśa manifested his form and said to the bhikṣu Huashou:
"The road is vast and remote, fraught with many dangers and difficulties; I, your disciple, shall escort you there so that your journey to and fro may be clear."
Auspicious. During the period before his return, a golden flower appeared in the air before the palace of Emperor Wen of Wei.
The Emperor asked the Grand Astrologer, "What strange omen is this? The Grand Astrologer divined and said, "The True Dharma of the Western Land is about to arrive here.
In less than a month, a Bhikṣu named Huishou will bring a golden flower from within his palm to this land. On the very first day of his arrival, the sky...
The golden flowers within the interior immediately vanished and were no longer seen. Since such a great omen had been manifested, his precepts and merit shall be transmitted forever.

As for the hermit Dai Yong, there was in the Jin dynasty a man from Qiaoguo named Dai Kui, whose courtesy name was Andao. His character was pure and his principles far-reaching; he directed his mind toward the teachings of the Buddha, and moreover, possessed keen spiritual faculties.
His thoughts were far-reaching and his ingenuity was such that he could rival the Creator.

As for his blending of ink, his application of colors, his carving of forms, and his intricate engraving techniques, even the subtle mastery of the people of Zhou or the exquisite skill with paper and silk of the guest from Song could not surpass him. Kui’s second son was Yong, styled Zhongruo;

his natural temperament was profound and serene, and he had a refined love for secluded gardens. Having already borne the burden of profound integrity, he also inherited his father’s ambition and artistic talent.
Whenever Sengqiu (逵) produced images, he would always consult with [Seng]yong on the matter. Jiang Yi of Jiyang had been friends with Sengyong since their youth.

Jiang Yi frequently requested that Sengyong create an image of Avalokiteśvara, exerting his full effort and thought to ensure it was perfect in every way. However, the physical features remained incomplete, and after many years, no success had been achieved.
Later, he dreamed of someone telling him: "Jiang Yi has no karmic affinity for Avalokiteśvara; you should change it to an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva."
Sengyong immediately stopped his hand and sent a letter to report this to Sengjiang. Before the messenger had even departed, Sengjiang’s letter arrived;

both had experienced a dream that same evening, and the accounts of their visions coincided exactly. Delighted by this divine response, Sengyong changed the name to Maitreya. Thereupon, the work came forth with effortless mastery;
without a moment’s deliberation, the radiant face was perfectly formed, completed in an instant. Those with discernment praised and revered it.
One realizes that the workings of causes and conditions are never errant. This image was formerly located at Longhua Temple in Kuaiji.

When comparing its craftsmanship to that of the two Dai brothers, it stands peerless throughout the ages. Many such images were produced, though they are now scattered across various temples, making it difficult to record them all in detail.

The Bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita was a native of Shan County in Kuaiji. Having left home at a young age, he applied himself with diligence and austere discipline; his observance of the precepts was strict and pure.
Later, he resided at Yinyue Temple on Mount Shicheng. To the north of the temple was a wall of green stone that rose straight up for more than several dozen zhang. When—
In the center was a form resembling the radiant light of a Buddha. Above it stood a grove of trees with curved trunks casting deep shade.

Whenever Hu reached the wall while reciting the sutras, he would invariably see the colors of the light shining brilliantly and hear the sounds of stringed instruments, pipes, songs, and hymns of praise.

"After my parinirvāṇa, among my disciples, if there are those who are diligent, cultivate various merits, do not fail in their dignified deportment, sweep the stupas and smear the ground with plaster, offer various famous incenses and exquisite flowers, practice various samādhis, enter deeply into right concentration (*samāpatti*), and recite the sūtras—such persons as these should go [to that realm]."

Even though their mental afflictions (*kleśa*) have not been severed, they should— as if they had attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*)— fix their mindfulness upon the physical form of the Buddha, recite the name of Maitreya, and perform such practices as these. If,
for even a single moment of thought, they observe the eightfold precepts, cultivate various pure deeds, and give rise to great vows, then after the end of their lives,
in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, they will immediately attain rebirth in Tuṣita.

"O Deva, you sit cross-legged upon a lotus flower. Five thousand devaputras perform celestial music and hold celestial māndārava flowers and mahāmāndārava flowers, scattering them over you, and praise you, saying: 'Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family, you have extensively cultivated meritorious deeds in Jambudvīpa and have been born here. This place is named Tuṣita.'"
"O Devendra, this present Lord of Devas is named Maitreya; you should take refuge in him. Upon hearing these words, he immediately prostrated.
Having prostrated, he gazed intently at the light of the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows and immediately attained transcendence from the sins of birth and death for ninety billion kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, according to their past affinities, preached the sublime Dharma for them, causing them to become firm and not regress from the mind set on the unsurpassed path.

Such sentient beings, if they purify all their karma and practice the six dharmas, will undoubtedly be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where they shall meet Maitreya; they will also follow Maitreya down to Jambudvīpa.
"Ānanda, this is the first hearing of the Dharma. In future ages, they shall encounter all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa;
they shall also encounter the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, during the Nakṣatra-kalpa. In the presence of these Buddhas, they shall receive the arousal of the bodhicitta. The Buddha told Upāli:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly of disciples, the eight classes of beings including devas and nāgas, and other such multitudes—"
If there are those who hear the name of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, and having heard it, rejoice, pay homage, and prostrate themselves, such persons, at the end of their lives,
will attain rebirth in that realm in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, no different from what was described before. Merely by hearing this name of Maitreya,
at the end of their lives they shall not fall into dark places, nor into borderlands of wrong views, nor into any evil states of discipline.
[One should maintain] proper deportment. Constantly give rise to right view. Accomplish the perfection of a retinue. Do not slander the Triple Gem.
If devas, nāgas, spirits, or ghosts should wish to be born in Tuṣita Heaven, they should perform this visualization and focus their mindfulness through contemplation.

They should keep the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts for one day up to seven days, contemplate the ten wholesome actions, and practice the path of the ten wholesome deeds. By means of these merits, [they should dedicate them...]
Those who aspire to be born in the presence of Maitreya should cultivate this contemplation.

For one who cultivates this contemplation, if they see even a single celestial being seated upon a lotus flower, or if for even a single moment of thought they invoke the name of Maitreya, this person shall eliminate the karmic offenses of birth and death accumulated over twelve hundred kalpas.
Merely hearing the name of Maitreya, joining their palms in reverence, and honoring him with devotion, this person shall eliminate five thousand kalpas [of such offenses].
Regarding the sins of birth and death: if there are those who pay homage to Maitreya, they shall be cleared of the sins of birth and death for ten billion kalpas.
Even if they are not reborn in heaven, in a future age beneath the Dragon-Flower Bodhi tree, they shall likewise encounter him, give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment, and attain the Way.
When the Buddha spoke these words, a vast multitude prostrated themselves at the feet of the Tathāgata and Maitreya, and circumambulated them.

They circumambulated him a hundred thousand times. Those who had not yet attained the Way each made a vow: "We, the eight classes of devas and humans, now before the Buddha, make this sincere and truthful vow:
may we, in a future age, encounter Maitreya; and after casting off these bodies, may we all attain rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven.
The World-Honored One prophesied, saying: "You and those in future ages who cultivate merit and uphold the precepts..."
All shall be reborn before Maitreya Bodhisattva and be taken into his care.
Those who practice this contemplation are said to have right contemplation; those who contemplate otherwise are said to have wrong contemplation.
The *Sūtra on the Previous Life of the Buddha Golden-Colored Monkey-Siṃhacandra* states: The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, among the assembly, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Vasumitra, who was wandering through the bamboo grove amidst the green trees.
Moving up and down, his voice was like that of a monkey; sometimes he spun three bells and performed the *nara* dance.
At that time, the local elders and travelers gathered in competition to watch him. When the crowd had assembled, he rose into the air, leapt to the top of a tree, and made monkey sounds.
Then eighty-four thousand golden monkeys from Vulture Peak Mountain gathered at the Bodhisattva’s location. The Bodhisattva...
He further performed various miraculous transformations to bring them joy.
At that time, the great assembly each said, "The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas acts like a child at play, deluding the masses with illusions. His conduct is so wicked that no one believes him;
he even commits unrighteous acts with birds and beasts. Such malicious rumors spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha. When the King heard these words, he felt resentment toward the [monks].
The King addressed the Śākya son, commanding the elder Kalandaka: "These Śākyas have gathered many monkeys within your park;
what are they doing? Does the Tathāgata know? The elder replied to the King:
"Vasu-mitra is performing a feat of transformation, causing the monkeys to rejoice all at once, and the devas are raining down flowers as an offering. Thus it was done.
"What is it? the ministers asked, for they did not know. At that time, the Great King, preceded and followed by his retinue, went to where the Buddha was.
From afar he saw the World-Honored One emitting a brilliant light like a mountain of purple gold; the entire assembled multitude was likewise the color of gold.
Venerable Madhu and the eighty-four thousand monkeys were also golden in color. Then the monkeys saw the Great King.
They arrived and performed various transformations; among them were those who gathered flowers and offered them to the Great King.

Upon seeing this, the Great King, together with the great assembly, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated before him, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What merit did these monkeys possess in their past lives that their bodies are golden in color? And what sin did they commit that they were born as animals?"

"Venerable Madhu, what merit did you plant in past lives that you were born into the family of a householder, renounced the world to study the Path, and yet what transgression have you committed that,
though born among humans with all faculties intact, you do not maintain the practice of precepts and keep company with monkeys,
such that the sound of your singing and speaking is exactly like that of a monkey, causing the non-Buddhists to laugh? I pray only that the World-Honored One will [explain this] for me."
"Please explain this so that I may attain understanding. The Buddha told the Great King: "Listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
In the distant past, immeasurable billions of kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Dīpaṃkara.

After that Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, there was a bhikṣu who practiced the Buddha-dharma amidst the mountains and marshes, firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts as a man protects his own eyes. Because of this..."
Having attained arhatship, he was at that time in a desolate marsh. There was a monkey who came to where the arhat was;
seeing the arhat sitting in meditation, absorbed in samādhi, it immediately took the arhat’s sitting mat and draped it over itself like a *kāṣāya*.

Following the manner of a śramaṇa, it bared its right shoulder, held an incense burner in its hand, and circumambulated the bhikṣu. At that time, the bhikṣu, having awakened from his samādhi, saw this...

The monkey possessed a virtuous mind and immediately snapped his fingers. He addressed the monkey, saying, "O son of the Dharma, you should now resolve to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
Upon hearing these words, the monkey was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated himself on the ground, bowing in reverence to the bhikṣu.
He further gathered flowers and scattered them over the bhikṣu. At that time, the bhikṣu immediately recited the Three Refuges for the monkey.
Then the monkey rose, joined his palms, and said: "Venerable One, I now wish to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
After the bhikṣu had administered the Three Refuges, he instructed him in repentance, leading him to fully confess his karmic offenses. Having attained arhatship, [the bhikṣu] was able to...
He eliminated the immeasurable heavy sins of sentient beings. Having thus performed the repentance three times with such earnestness, he addressed the monkey, saying:
"Son of the Dharma, you are now pure; this is what is called a Bodhisattva. From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, having received the five precepts, you shall seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the monkey, having received the teachings according to the instructions and finished making his vow, leaped about with great joy and ran away.

He climbed a high mountain and fell from a suspended tree to his death. Because he had received the five precepts and thereby severed his karma as an animal, he was immediately reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he encountered a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood (Ekajātipratibaddha). The Bodhisattva expounded for him the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.
He then took celestial flowers and descended into a marshy glade to make offerings to an Arhat Bhikṣu. Upon seeing this, the Arhat smiled and addressed him, saying, "O Heavenly King!"
"The retribution for good and evil follows one like a shadow follows a form; they never depart from each other.
The Devaputra Monkey addressed him, saying, "Virtuous One, in my previous life, what karmic offenses did I commit to be born among monkeys? And by what merit did I encounter you, Virtuous One?"
He escaped birth as an animal and was reborn in the heavens. The Arhat replied:
"In the distant past, in this Jambudvīpa, there appeared a Buddha named Ratnaprajñā Tathāgata.

After his parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma (Śāsanapratirūpaka), there was a bhikṣu named Padmagarbha who frequently formed close friendships with kings, elders, and householders, yet lived by wrong livelihoods."
Deceitful and crooked, failing to maintain the practice of the precepts, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
There they suffer all manner of torments for eighteen kalpas, like a blooming lotus, with a lifespan of one kalpa; when that kalpa ends, they are reborn again.
Thus they pass through various great hells for eighty-four thousand kalpas. Emerging from the hells, they fall among the hungry ghosts, swallowing and drinking molten copper.
After eighty-four thousand years, he emerged from the realm of hungry ghosts and was reborn successively among cattle, pigs, dogs, and monkeys for five hundred lifetimes each.
Because of his prior offerings and his solemn vow to uphold the precepts, he has now encountered me once more and attained birth in the heavens.
The bhikṣu who upheld the precepts was none other than my own self; the bhikṣu who was negligent was none other than you. Having heard this, the Devaputra Monkey—
When these words were spoken, his heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end. He repented of his former transgressions and immediately returned to the heavens.
The Buddha said to the Great King, "That monkey, though he was an animal, upon seeing an Arhat, received and upheld the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.

By virtue of this prior merit, he transcended a thousand kalpas of extremely evil and heavy karma to be reborn in the heavens, where he encountered a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood."
"Sā. From this time forward, he shall encounter countless Buddhas, purely cultivate the Brahma-faring, fulfill the six pāramitās, and abide on the stage of non-retrogression.
In his final body, following after Maitreya, he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; his Buddha-name shall be Siṃhacandra Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "If you wish to know who this future Buddha Siṃhacandra is, it is this person within the present assembly."
"He is the bhikṣu Vasumitra. Upon hearing these words, the king immediately rose, joined his palms, and broke into a sweat all over his body.

Weeping with tears falling like rain, he repented and reproached himself. He prostrated himself before Vasumitra, touching his head to the ground to pay homage at the bhikṣu’s feet, and confessed his prior transgressions.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "If you wish to know who these eighty-four thousand golden monkeys were..."
As for the monkey: in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were eighty-four thousand bhikṣuṇīs between two countries, Vārāṇasī and Kauśāmbī.
They practiced various unrighteous acts and violated the heavy prohibitions;
they were mad, foolish, and without wisdom, like deluded monkeys. When they saw virtuous bhikṣus, they looked upon them as thieves. At that time, there was an arhat bhikṣu...
The bhikṣuṇī was named Shan-yan-yin (Svastyāśaya). [The other bhikṣuṇīs] both preached the Dharma for her, yet she again harbored resentment and malice.

At that time, the arhat bhikṣuṇī, seeing that these wicked people did not give rise to wholesome thoughts, immediately gave rise to compassion. She ascended into the void and performed the eighteen transformations.
When those wicked people saw these miraculous manifestations, each removed a golden ring and scattered them over the arhat bhikṣuṇī, vowing: "In birth after birth, may our bodies..."

They became golden in color. They now repent for all the evil deeds they previously committed. At that time, those wicked people, their bodies destroyed and their lives ended, fell into the Avīci Hell.
Passing through it in succession for ninety-two kalpas, they remained constantly in hell. Finally, they emerged from the hell.
For five hundred lifetimes, they were constantly reborn as hungry ghosts (*preta*). Emerging from that state, for one thousand lifetimes, they were always born as golden-colored monkeys.

Great King, you should know that those eighty-four thousand nuns who violated the precepts and reviled the *arhatī* at that time are these eighty-four thousand golden monkeys present in this assembly today. At that time, [those who] provided...
"The one who supported those wicked bhikṣuṇīs is you, Great King, today. These monkeys, due to the influence of past habits, carry flowers and incense to make offerings to the Great King.
Those who defiled those bhikṣuṇīs at that time are today Kokālika and the five hundred eunuchs of the king.
The Buddha said to the Great King, "One must not fail to be careful regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind. At that time...
Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, the king repented before the Buddha, feeling shame and self-reproach. His mind was suddenly liberated, and he attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
The eight thousand people who had accompanied the king sought ordination under the Buddha and all became *arhats*.

The remaining sixteen thousand people all resolved to attain *bodhicitta*, as did eighty thousand devas. Furthermore, eighty-four thousand golden-colored [beings] likewise resolved their minds [upon enlightenment].
The monkeys, hearing of their past causes and conditions, felt shame and reproached themselves. They circumambulated the Buddha a thousand times and confessed their transgressions before him.

Each of them resolved to attain unexcelled bodhicitta; according to the length of their respective lifespans, after their deaths they shall be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where they will meet Maitreya and attain the stage of non-retrogression.
This shall continue for more than a million billion nayutas of asaṃkhyeya Ganges-sands of eons.
After eighty-four thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they shall attain Buddhahood, appearing in the world one after another throughout a single kalpa named Mahāprabha.

They shall share the same Buddha-name, all being called Tathāgata Suvarṇaprabhāsa. (In ancient times, birds and beasts that were able to speak did so because their time spent fallen into the bodies of animals was brief;
those who cannot speak now have done so because they have wandered through the realms of hell and the animal path for a long duration, and thus are unable to understand human speech.)
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Do you now see these two hundred goddesses who join their palms in reverent salutation to the Tathāgata?
Ānanda replied, "I have seen them. The Buddha said, "These goddesses have already, in the past..."
In the past, at the sites of five hundred Buddhas, they deeply planted roots of goodness. From this point onward, they shall again make offerings to countless Buddhas.
After the passing of seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they shall all attain Buddhahood, named Pure King (*Śuddharāja*).
Following the end of their lives, these goddesses shall transform their female bodies and all be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven to make offerings.
Regarding the service of Maitreya Bodhisattva,

the *Jingtongsheng jing* (Sūtra on the Birth of the Youth) states: At that time, there were five hundred young boys who formed a companionship and played together every day, until they all arrived at a river.
