They gathered sand to build stupas, each saying, "My stupa is beautiful. Though they all possessed virtuous hearts, their merit from past lives was thin.
At that time, the heavens suddenly sent down rain, and the river waters surged violently; they were swept away and drowned. The Buddha told the assembly:

"The five hundred youths have been reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where they have all together resolved to practice the path of a bodhisattva. The Buddha then emitted a radiance, enabling their parents to see their sons.
The Buddha called out from afar to the five hundred young sons of gods, "Come! and they all arrived immediately, remaining suspended in mid-air.
They scattered flowers before the Buddha and prostrated themselves, saying, "By the grace of the World-Honored One, although our bodies have perished, we have been able to behold Maitreya Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Excellent! You have made a most fortunate resolve. You have known the Way of the Ultimate Truth and established stūpas and monasteries; because of this..."
He was reborn in heaven, where he beheld Maitreya and received his instructions on the Dharma. The Buddha preached a sutra for him, and all were filled with joy;

they established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression. Each addressed their parents, saying, "Do not grieve or suffer any longer; exert yourselves with diligence and cultivate yourselves through the Dharma. Their parents all resolved to seek the Way.
The devaputra paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, and suddenly vanished, returning to Tuṣita Heaven.
The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Contemplation of the Mind-ground of Beasts) states: In a past age, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa spoke these verses for the sake of various beasts:
"This body is the root of suffering; All other sufferings are its branches and leaves. If one can sever the root of suffering,"

All sufferings shall be entirely removed. Regarding the karma of your past lives, you committed transgressions with a heart that felt no remorse, thereby incurring immeasurable retribution—bodies of various forms that endure suffering.
If you give rise to a heart of profound earnestness and seek repentance for even a single moment, all your sins will be utterly extinguished, like fire consuming mountains and marshes.
"This body is suffering and impure; it is without self and impermanent.
You all should give rise to a heart of profound weariness and detachment.
At that time, immeasurable birds and beasts, having heard these verses, repented with utmost sincerity in a single thought-moment.

He immediately abandoned the evil realms and was reborn in the Fourth Heaven. There he paid homage to a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood, heard the Dharma of non-retrogression, and attained ultimate Nirvana.
Thus did the jackal.
The *Adbhuta-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* states: Long ago, on Mount Sita in the kingdom of Vimala, there was a jackal who, being pursued by a lion, fell into a wild well on a hillock.
Having remained there for three days, resigned to his death, he spoke these verses:
All things are impermanent; alas, I did not offer sustenance to the lion. Alas, this body is beset by the calamity of death;
though I craved life, my efforts were in vain. That my efforts were in vain is already regrettable, yet I have further defiled the waters of the human realm.
I repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions; may you deign to illuminate my heart. For all the evil karma committed in previous lives.
He caused all current debts to be paid in full; from this point on, he encountered an enlightened teacher.

When he had practiced until he attained Buddhahood, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard of this and, accompanied by eighty thousand devas, went to the side of the well and said: "We have not heard the holy teaching."
"Having long dwelt in the darkness and obscurity, you previously spoke as if you were no ordinary being; I pray that you will further proclaim the Dharma. The jackal replied:

"O Lord of Devas, you lack instruction and do not recognize the propriety of the occasion. The Dharma Master is below, yet you place yourself above him; you have not first cultivated reverence, yet you inquire after the essentials of the Dharma."

Śakra then received him with celestial robes and prostrated himself in repentance. He recalled that in the past, he had seen people of the world first prepare a high seat and later invite a Dharma Master;
immediately, the various devas would each remove their precious robes and pile them up to form a high seat for the master to ascend.
Śakra said, "There are two great causes and conditions: first, preaching the Dharma to enlighten and transform humans and devas, so that their merit may be inexhaustible."

Because it is a matter of measure. Second, it is to repay the kindness of being provided with food. The Heavenly Lord said: "To have escaped the calamity of the well is a great reward for one's merit;

how can it be said that the kindness [of the donor] does not reach [the recipient]? He replied: "In the cycle of birth and death, each has its own destiny. Some people crave life, while others welcome death.
There are foolish people who do not know that after death there is rebirth; they turn away from the Buddha-dharma and fail to encounter an enlightened teacher."
"Those who covet life and fear death fall into hell when they die. A person of wisdom serves the Triple Gem, encounters an enlightened teacher, reforms their evils, and cultivates goodness.
Such a person welcomes death and fears birth; upon dying, they are reborn in the heavens.

The Heavenly Emperor said, "As Your Reverence has taught, if one’s life cannot be preserved through merit, I pray to hear about the giving of food and the giving of Dharma. He replied, "To bestow gifts upon those who are hungry is [the giving of food]."
One who bestows precious jewels provides for the needs of a single day;

one who bestows the Dharma through teaching and transformation can cause sentient beings to enter the supramundane path, attain the fruits of the Three Vehicles, escape the three evil realms, and enjoy the bliss of humans and devas.
For this reason, the Buddha taught that the merit of giving the Dharma is immeasurable. The Heavenly Lord said: "Master, now..."
"Is this form the result of karmic retribution, or is it a manifested transformation? He replied, "It is the fruit of sin; it is not a manifestation.
The Lord of Devas said, "I took him to be a sage, yet now I hear he is subject to the retribution of sin. I do not know the reason for this; I pray you tell me the causes and conditions.

He replied, "In the past, when I was born in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, in the city of Padmāvatī, I was the son of a poor family of the Kṣatriya caste. From my youth, I possessed exceptional intelligence and clarity."
He was fond of learning. By the age of twelve, he followed his teacher into the mountains, never missing the proper seasons for study.
Over fifty years, there were no among the ninety-six types of scriptures that he did not master; all this was due to the kindness of his Upādhyāya, whose merit is difficult to repay.

Having first cultivated wisdom, he came to know his own past lives. However, upon receiving the royal throne, he became indulgent, licentious, and attached to pleasure. When his karmic retribution was exhausted, his life ended, and he was reborn...

[The realms of] hell and animals... (From here on, as stated at length, it is omitted). At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with eighty thousand devas, having received the ten wholesome precepts, wished to return to the celestial palace.
He asked, "Preceptor, when will you cast off this retribution of sin and attain birth in the heavens?
The jackal replied, "In seven days from now, I shall cast off this body and be born in Tuṣita Heaven. You all should likewise vow to be born there."
In that heaven, many bodhisattvas were preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings.

At that time, the jackal focused his mind single-mindedly on the practice of the ten virtuous paths and did not go out to seek food. When his life ended after seven days, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven palace.

He immediately recognized his past lives and again used the ten virtues to teach and transform the various devas. (The jackal resembles a fox but is smaller; its color is bluish-yellow like a dog; it nests upon high cliffs and tall trees.)
At that time, the Elder Sudatta (also known as Anāthapiṇḍika) went with Śāriputra outside the city of Śrāvastī to plan the site for the vihāra.
Sudatta held one end of the measuring cord in his own hand, while Śāriputra held the other end; together they traversed the grounds of the vihāra. At that time, Śāriputra...
Vimalakīrti smiled with delight. Sudatta asked, "Venerable sir, why do you smile?

He replied, "As soon as you began to prepare the ground for this sūtra, the palaces within the six heavens of the desire realm were already completed. I have lent you my divine eye, through which you can see all the magnificent and pure palaces of the six heavens.
He then asked Śāriputra, "Among the six heavens, which place is the most pleasant? Śāriputra replied, "The three lower [heavens]..."
The color of the sky was dyed [with light]. The upper two heavens were characterized by arrogance and negligence, whereas in the fourth heaven, there was little desire and contentment;

a Bodhisattva bound for one more birth (ekajātipratibaddha) constantly comes to be born therein, so that the teaching of the Dharma never ceases. Sudatta said, "I shall indeed be reborn in the fourth heaven.
As soon as these words were finished, all the other palaces vanished, and only the palace of the fourth heaven remained serene and radiant. Miscellaneous...
The *Āgama* scriptures state that when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada fell ill, the Buddha went in person to visit him and prophesied that he would attain the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
Upon his death, he was reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where he constantly descended to pay homage to the Buddha and listen to the Dharma before returning to the celestial realm.
(This account refers to his outward manifestation, describing his attainment of a minor fruit; however, if one speaks of his actual reality, he is a great *bodhisattva*.)
The Bodhisattvas Asaṅga and Vasubandhu (Vasubandhu was formerly called Tianqin):
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga was a native of Gandhāra in India. He lived during the millennium following the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.
Manifesting his spiritual power, he appeared in this world; having encountered the Dharma, he awakened to the Way. He left the household life and studied under the Mūlasarvāstivāda school.
After some time, he turned his faith toward the Mahāyāna. His younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, left the household life and received instruction in the Sarvāstivāda school.

Possessing vast learning and a powerful memory, he mastered all branches of knowledge and refined his intellectual faculties. As for Aśvaghoṣa’s disciple Buddhasiṃha (translated into Chinese as Shizi Jue, or "Lion Awakening"), he was [a master of] esoteric...

His conduct was unfathomable and his exceptional talent was renowned. Two or three other worthy sages would often say to one another, "In practicing our spiritual disciplines, we aspire to behold Maitreya.
If any of us should first depart this life and succeed in fulfilling our long-held wish, you must inform the others so that we may know where he has gone.
Subsequently, Siṃhabuddhi passed away first, yet for three years there was no report from him. Vasubandhu Bodhisattva soon followed in death.

Six months passed, yet there was still no response. At that time, all the non-Buddhists mocked them, saying that the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and Siṃhabuddhi had transmigrated into evil realms and thus lacked spiritual discernment.

Subsequently, during the first watch of the night, while the Bodhisattva Asaṅga was instructing his disciples in the methods of meditative concentration, the lamp light suddenly dimmed and the sky became brilliantly illuminated. There was...
One day, a celestial being descended through the air and entered the courtyard, where he paid respectful homage to Asaṅga.
Asaṅga asked, "Why have you come so late? What is your name now? He replied, "Since leaving this life, I have gone to Tuṣita Heaven.
Among the inner retinue of Maitreya, I was born within a lotus flower. As soon as the lotus opened, Maitreya praised me, saying: 'Welcome, O Vipaśyanāmati! Welcome!'"
"Vipula-mati, as soon as you had completed one circuit, you returned to report. The Bodhisattva Asaṅga asked: 'Where is Siṃhabuddhi now?
He replied: 'While I was circumambulating, I saw Siṃhabuddhi among the assembly outside, deeply attached to celestial pleasures.'"

There was no leisure for mutual consultation, so how could we have been able to come and report this? The Bodhisattva Asaṅga said: "This matter is already concluded. What are the marks of Maitreya, and what Dharma does he proclaim? [The other] replied:
"As for the marks and signs of Maitreya, words cannot fully describe them. Regarding the sublime Dharma he proclaims, its meaning is no different from this.
However, the wondrous purport of the Bodhisattva is clear, flowing, harmonious, and elegant; those who hear it forget their fatigue, and those who receive it never grow weary. Thus it was said.

It is said: "People nowadays all claim that Siṃhabuddhi was afflicted by an attachment to celestial pleasures, regarding this as his 'sickness. However, his birth in Tuṣita was originally for the purpose of seeking an audience with Maitreya, personally receiving the Master’s teachings, and awakening to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

How could he have sought celestial pleasures? Since he lacked any thought of attachment to pleasure, why worry that he would not be born among the inner assembly [of Tuṣita]? Furthermore, when Siṃhabuddhi first resolved his mind on his vow, who could have known what he prayed for? Since it is said that his secret practices were unfathomable, how can they be subject to conceptual speculation?"
Dharma Master Dao’an’s surname was Wei, and he was a native of Fuyi in Changshan. He left home to become a monk at a young age. For three years, he performed manual labor on the farm;

he applied himself with diligence to his toil, never showing even the slightest hint of resentment. Only after several more years did he finally request scriptures from his teacher, who granted them to him.

The *Bianyi jing* (Sūtra on Discerning Intent) consists of one fascicle and comprises approximately five thousand words. Dao’an took this sūtra with him into the fields; while resting there, he took it up for reading.

At dusk, upon returning home, he returned the sūtra to his teacher and requested another. The teacher said, "You have not yet finished reading yesterday’s sūtra; why do you seek more today? He replied: [as follows].

He then recited it from memory without looking at the text. Although his teacher marveled at this, he did not yet believe him. He gave him another copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra), a volume of slightly less than ten thousand words, and he carried it away as before.
At dusk, he returned it to his teacher. When the teacher held the scripture and compared it against his recitation, there was not a single character that differed.
The teacher was greatly astonished and marveled at his extraordinary talent. Later, he conferred the full ordination upon him and allowed him to travel freely to study. He eventually reached Ye.

He encountered Fotudeng, who saw him and sighed in admiration. He conversed with him all day long. When the assembly saw that his physical appearance did not match his bearing, they all looked down on him.
Fotudeng remarked with wonder, "This man possesses far-reaching insight; he is not your peer. Consequently, he served Fotudeng as his teacher. Fotudeng then gave a lecture.
Dao’an frequently recited and expounded [these texts]. Later, he resided at Shoudu Monastery, where his followers numbered several hundred; he constantly proclaimed the Dharma and transformed others.

His commentaries on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Dàoxíng* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā), the *Mìmì* (Guhyakādhipati), the *Ānāpāna*, and various other sutras all involved examining the wording and comparing the phrases to establish the meaning of their origins and conclusions, as well as analyzing doubts and providing detailed exegesis.
These works comprise twenty-two fascicles; their introductory prefaces are profound and rich, exquisitely exhausting the deep purport, and are systematically organized.
Once the prefaces were composed, the literary principles were harmoniously integrated and the meaning of the scriptures was clearly elucidated; this began with Dao’an.
At that time, Fu Jian dispatched envoys to present one statue each of foreign gold, pearl-encrusted Maitreya, gold-thread embroidery, and woven silk images.

Later, he resided at Wuchong Temple in Chang’an, where his assembly numbered several thousand. He extensively propagated the Dharma and its transformation. Previously, the śramaṇas of the Wei and Jin dynasties had relied upon...
The Master’s family name was Shi. Thus, their surnames were each different. Dao’an considered that among all the great teachers, none surpassed Śākyamuni as the Honored One;
he therefore took "Śākya" as his clan name. Later, he obtained the *Ekottarika Āgama*, which indeed stated that the four rivers flow into the sea.
There was no longer any mention of "rivers" (the *śroṇa*); those of the four castes who became śramaṇas were all designated as members of the Śākya clan (*śākyavaṃśa*).

Since this corresponded perfectly with the sūtras, it was subsequently established as a permanent standard. Dao’an frequently made vows together with his disciples, such as Fayu, before Maitreya, pledging to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
Later, on the twenty-seventh day of the first month in the twenty-first year of the Jianyuan era of the Qin dynasty, a strange monk suddenly arrived at the temple seeking lodging.
As the temple rooms were cramped, he was accommodated in the lecture hall. At that time, the *karmadāna* (rector) was on duty in the main hall.

At night, he saw this monk entering and exiting through a crack in the window. He immediately informed Dao’an about it. Startled, Dao’an rose to pay his respects and inquired about the monk’s purpose for coming.
The monk replied, "I have come for your sake. Dao’an said, "I consider my own transgressions to be so deep; how could I possibly be delivered? The monk answered, "You can certainly be delivered.
However, you must bathe the Holy Monk (Śāriputra) once more, and your vow will surely be fulfilled. He then provided a detailed explanation of the bathing ritual. Dao’an...

He asked about his future life and the place where he would be reborn. Thereupon, he gestured with his hand toward the northwest of the sky, and immediately the clouds parted, revealing the magnificent and wondrous realm of Tuṣita in its entirety.
That evening, several dozen members of the assembly all witnessed this together.
Later, while preparing bathing implements, An saw an extraordinary young boy arrive at the temple with dozens of companions to play.

After a short while, he proceeded to bathe; this was indeed a holy manifestation. On the eighth day of the second month of that year, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "I am about to depart.
That day, after the midday meal, he passed away without illness. When Dao’an was first born, a piece of skin about an inch wide grew upon his left arm;
it adhered to the arm and could be moved up and down by stroking it, but it could not be removed from the hand. Later, Master Xuan...
He questioned a celestial deity and learned that An was the Bodhisattva Seal-Hand (Mudrāhasta).
Dharma Master Zhu Sengfu was a native of Ye.
From his youth, he maintained the precepts and his resolve was firm and arduous. His learning encompassed all the treatises, and he was also proficient in the sutras and the Dharma.
His Way flourished in the Yi and Luo regions, and the capital’s populace followed him as their teacher.

Encountering the famine and turmoil of the Western Jin, he and Shi Dao’an and others went into seclusion at Huozhai, where they refined their studies and engaged in analytical inquiry until they thoroughly mastered the subtle and profound mysteries.

Later, while residing at Shangming Temple in Jingzhou, he lived frugally on simple vegetables, performing prostrations and repentance with fervent devotion, vowing to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven to behold Maitreya. At that time, Wang Chen of Langye served as—
The Imperial Protector of Jingzhou, hearing that Sengfu was pure and austere in character, invited him to serve as his preceptor for the precepts. His entire family followed and honored him.
Two days before he passed away, he suddenly said, "I shall depart tomorrow. At the time of his death, a wondrous fragrance filled the room and the sounds of Sanskrit chanting resounded in succession.
Monastics and laypeople rushed to see him; those who came numbered in the tens of thousands. In the afternoon of that day, he passed away without illness at the age of sixty. [Precepts]
I have not yet heard of [the account of] Falü.

Dharma Master Tanguai, whose other name was Huijing, was surnamed Zhuo and was a native of Nanyang. Living in poverty, he devoted himself to study and applied his mind to the ancient classics and scriptures. Later, he heard...
Dharma Master Fadao was lecturing on the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*. [The master] borrowed a robe to listen to it once; he subsequently attained a profound realization of Buddhist principles.
He abandoned secular life to follow the Way, serving Master Dao’an as his teacher. He became extensively versed in the Tripiṭaka and recited over five hundred thousand words of scripture.

Every day he performed five hundred prostrations before the Buddha. The Prince of Linchuan of the Jin dynasty held him in high esteem. Later, when he fell gravely ill, he constantly recited the name of Maitreya.

The name of the Buddha never ceased from his mind or mouth. While his disciple Zhisheng was attending to him during his illness, he asked, "Why do you not aspire to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang)?
Sengjie replied, "I and eight others, including the Upādhyāya, made a vow together to be reborn in Tuṣita. The Upādhyāya, Daoyuan, and the others have all already been reborn above;
I alone have not yet attained that state. It is for this reason that I still maintain my vow. As soon as he finished speaking, light immediately shone upon his body.
Her appearance became even more radiant, and she then suddenly passed away. She was seventy years of age and was buried to the right of Master Dao’an’s tomb.

Nun Huizao, whose original surname was Lu, was a native of Wu Commandery; she was the daughter of Dao’an’s younger sister. When Huizao was over ten years old, her body was afflicted with a severe illness.
"Excellent medicine must be administered; it will increase daily without causing harm. At that time, Shi Faji of Taixuantai Temple said to An Xun:
"I fear this illness arises from karma and cannot be eliminated by medical means.

According to the scriptures I have consulted, if one encounters peril and suffering and can take refuge in the Triple Gem, repenting and making vows, all shall obtain salvation. You should be able to join your daughter in renouncing all heterodox practices."
Layperson: "If you wash away the defilements and focus your mind single-mindedly, you shall surely recover and find peace and tranquility.

He then installed an image of Avalokiteśvara within his residence. Purifying his heart and cleansing his intent, he venerated it with utmost sincerity. Suffering from illness, he prostrated himself and maintained continuous, focused recollection for seven days.
During the first watch of the night, he suddenly saw a golden image about one chi in height, which stroked his body from head to [feet].
Her feet were healed, and her chronic illness was suddenly and completely cured. Having personally experienced such spiritual efficacy, she subsequently requested ordination.

She practiced with diligent and tireless effort, reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, maintaining a vegetarian diet and lifelong celibacy for thirty-seven years. She constantly directed her mind and focused her thoughts on the aspiration to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, while reciting the name of Maitreya Buddha, she passed away in silence.

Nun Guangjing, whose secular surname was Hu and given name Dao bi, was a native of Dongqian in Wuxing. She entered the monastic life in her youth and followed her teacher to reside at Zhong Temple in Guangling.

From a young age, Jing was rigorous in her conduct; as she grew older, she devoted herself to the practice of dhyāna. She abstained from sweet and fatty foods. She was about to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

He abstained from grain and subsisted on pine nuts. After observing the precepts for fifteen years, although his mental faculties remained sharp and clear, his physical strength was utterly exhausted.
His prayers were so sincere and earnest that he frequently experienced supernatural responses, which occurred every month and every new moon. The śramaṇa Facheng said to him:

Jing heard that consuming [medicinal herbs] was not a flourishing practice of the Buddha, so he returned to eating polished rice. He redoubled his vigor and applied himself to study with tireless diligence.

Those who followed him to learn the practice of contemplation numbered about a hundred at all times. In the fifth month of the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he fell ill and said, "I have long been weary of this body and its suffering.
Thereupon, he performed repentance while prostrating in his illness, never ceasing from his heart or his lips. By nature...
His principles were tranquil and clear; his spirit and vital energy were serene and ethereal. On the first day of the nineteenth year, he ceased all intake of grain and drink.

He focused his thoughts on Tuṣita Heaven with an uninterrupted continuity of mind. Thus it continued until the night of the eighth day of the fourth month, when extraordinary fragrances and marvelous signs filled the void of space.
That night, he entered parinirvāṇa.

The nun Huiqiong, surnamed Qiong, was originally from Zhong in Guangzhou. Her conduct was lofty and pure; she abstained from fish and meat. Approaching eighty years of age, her aspirations were fixed upon Maitreya.
She constantly wore clothing made of hemp and flax, never wearing silk or cotton. She managed the affairs of the monastery while also engaging in lecturing and preaching.
In the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era, Lady Wang, the mother of the Heir Apparent of the Prince of Jiangxia of the Song dynasty, donated land to Sengqiong.
Sengqiong established it as a monastery, naming it Nan Yong’an Temple. In the twenty-second year, Xiao Chengzhi of Lanling erected a foreign-style stupa there.
In the fifteenth year of the Yuanjia era, Sengqiong had founded Bodhi Temple, complete with its halls, pavilions, and courtyards.
All were magnificent and beautiful. In the twenty-fourth year of the Yuanjia era, he followed Meng Yi to Kuaiji and instructed his disciples, saying:
"After my death, there is no need to bury me. You may borrow someone to flay my body so that living beings may feed upon it until it is completely consumed.

Unable to bear the thought of being slaughtered and cut up, he then informed the Magistrate of Juong County, Yu Zhu, and had him place [his remains] in the mountains so that birds and beasts might [feed upon them].
He took it himself and ate it. After more than ten days had passed, [the corpse] remained as it was before, its complexion unchanged.
He ordered villagers to scatter rice near the corpse; the birds ate the rice from a distance, yet the grains near the corpse all remained there.
His disciple Huilang, hearing of this in the capital, rushed to welcome him back. They returned him for burial on a ridge in front of Gaozuo Temple, where a stupa was erected upon the tomb. (Jiong 1)

She cultivated the precepts with austerity from birth and set her heart’s aspiration on Maitreya; thus, she attained a death that distinguished her from ordinary people, serving as clear evidence of her rebirth in the Pure Land.
Nun Jingxiu:

her original surname was Liang, and she was a native of Anding. Her grandfather, Chou, served as the Commandant of the Pacification Army (Zhenglü Sīmǎ), and her father, Canzhi, was the Prefectural Governor of Longchuan County.
Hou Xiu was intelligent and sagacious from childhood and delighted in practicing compassion and benevolence. At the age of seven, he naturally began to observe the fasts.
When his family invited a monk to recite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he heard the prohibition against fish and meat and immediately adopted a vegetarian diet. He followed the foreign śramaṇa Puli.
She received and accepted the five precepts, upholding them with diligent devotion. She performed prostrations, recited the scriptures, and practiced day and night without ceasing.

At the age of twelve, she sought to leave the household life, but her parents forbade her. Once she was able to write, she constantly transcribed the sutras herself. It was not until she reached the age of twenty-nine that she finally obtained permission to do so.
She became a disciple of the head nun of Qingyuan Temple and served her teacher with the utmost sincerity, yet she remained fearful that she might still fall short. Part three.
She diligently cultivated her karma, never flagging from morning until night. Whenever she was assigned monastic duties or communal labor, she always took the lead.

Whether traveling long distances or engaged in various affairs, whether moving forward or pausing, looking up or down, she invariably adhered to the monastic rules and regulations. Consequently, benevolent deities venerated and protected her, remaining constantly by her side.
At that time, there was Master Ma, whom the world called a "divine man. Upon seeing Xiu, he remarked: "This nun shall be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven."
Once, while three people were seated together inside the Buddha Hall, they suddenly heard a sound from the air that resembled the bellowing of an ox.

The other two were struck with terror, but Xiu remained unperturbed. He returned to his quarters, took a candle, and ascended the steps; as he did so, he again heard a voice from the air saying, "The nuns, clear the path!
Zen Master Xiu is returning. Later, while sitting together with some nuns, one nun rose briefly to return to her room and saw—
One person clapped his hands and stopped him, saying, "Do not disturb the nun Xiù. She wishes to invite Dharma Master Huī to lecture on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
However, she has only one thousand coins and fears the matter will not be accomplished. That night, he dreamed that geese, magpies, starlings, and sparrows each rode in a carriage.
Large and small [vessels] were provided according to their size; everyone raised their voices in unison, saying, "I shall assist Master Xiù in his lecture.

When it came time for the preparations, seventy donors vied with one another to provide exquisite offerings. In the seventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, the foreign śramaṇa Guṇavarman arrived at the capital.

His discipline and conduct were pure and lofty, so Xiù further received the precepts from him. Wearing hempen robes and subsisting on a diet of simple beans, they lived together in a community of more than ten people.
They all took meditative concentration as their primary practice. Xiu transcribed various sutras with his own hand and established a separate scripture platform within the monastery.

The two brothers, the Nāga Kings Sāgara and [his sibling], manifested their presence for many days to demonstrate their protection. Among those who came and went, there was no one who did not see them.
Whenever he offered fruit and food to the noble Saṃgha, there were invariably miraculous signs. Furthermore, he once made offerings for seven days.
Yang performed prostrations and repentance while kneeling in the Hu-style. Concentrating his mind and focusing his thoughts, he immediately saw two Brahma monks raising their hands and conversing;
one was named Mikhaka and the other was named Vighra. The *kāṣāya* robes they wore were the color of ripe mulberries.
Xiu then dyed his robes with mud so that their color matched what he had seen. On another day, he again invited five hundred Arhats from Lake Anavatapta. Furthermore...

He invited five hundred arhats from Kasmira as well as the great virtuous ones (mahābhadanta) of the capital. When they saw a single brahmin monk, the entire assembly was suspicious and questioned him immediately.
He replied, "I have come from Kasmira. Yet, after he had walked only ten or so paces, he suddenly vanished.
Furthermore, when he bathed the holy monks, both their inner and outer states were tranquil; there was only the sound of the ladle being rinsed. All such auspicious wonders were of this nature.
Emperor Wenhui of the Qi dynasty and Prince Wenxuan of Jingling treated him with great courtesy and provided him with constant offerings and support.
As he grew old and his strength failed, he could no longer travel; they permitted him to ride in a carriage to the inner palace.

On the seventeenth day of the sixth month in the fifth year, he suffered from a severe mental affliction and ceased eating or drinking. On the nineteenth day of the sixth month, Dharma Master Huiquan of Pengcheng Temple had a dream.
He saw a single-pillar hall, its magnificence and beauty beyond compare, which he took to be the palace of the Tuṣita Heaven. Within it, he saw Jingxiu;

Faxian then entrusted him entirely with the matter, saying, "May you be reborn in this wondrous place and not forget to welcome me. Jingxiu replied, "The Dharma Master is a man of great character who propagates the sutras and teachings;
by your own merit, you should dwell in such a superior realm. Later, when Jingxiu fell ill, Faxian went to visit him and recounted the events of his dream. This continued until the seventh day.
On the thirteenth day of the month, for a short while, he dreamed that banners, canopies, and musical instruments were located to the northwest of the Buddha hall.
On the twentieth day, he took leave of his circle of acquaintances and fellow monks. On the twenty-seventh day, he said to his disciples, "I shall ascend to the Tuṣita Heaven palace.

Having finished speaking, he passed away at the age of eighty-nine. (The Sūtra says: "If there are bhikṣus or any of the great assembly who do not weary of birth and death, but delight in being born in heaven...")

Those who revere the unsurpassed bodhicitta and wish to become disciples of Maitreya should practice this contemplation. Those who practice this contemplation should uphold the five precepts, the eightfold fast, and the full monastic precepts; they should be diligent in body and mind, refrain from seeking the severance of fetters, and cultivate the ten wholesome dharmas.

They should contemplate, one by one, the supreme and exquisite bliss of the Tuṣita Heaven. To contemplate in this way is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called wrong contemplation.

As for "not seeking the severance of fetters," these are Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas who remain with afflictions (*kleśa*) to deliver sentient beings, unlike the followers of the Two Vehicles who attain realization, extinguish their bodies, and enter the nirvāṇa of severed wisdom. It is like Bi Yao and Xiu, who focused their minds and concentrated their thoughts; by practicing contemplation according to the sūtras, the sacred realm manifested before them.

Dharma Master Yancong’s secular surname was Li; he was a native of Bo in Zhao Commandery. His family had long been known as a distinguished lineage of scholar-officials, and his clan was celebrated as one of the foremost aristocratic houses. From his youth, he was intelligent and quick-witted;

his literary talent was fresh and elegant. His insight penetrated the profound and subtle, and his character was as clear as water or a mirror. He perceived things at a glance, and few matters escaped his notice.
To provide further detail: when he first arrived in Xindu, the monk Master Bian had him recite the *Sudāna-sūtra*, which consists of fewer than seven thousand words;
he completed it in a single day. He then recited the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*, which he also mastered in several days. By the time he reached the age of ten, [he had achieved this].
Only then was he permitted to leave the household life and given the name Daojiang. Because his wisdom and reputation spread far and wide like the currents of a great river, he was so named.
At the beginning of the Wuping era of the Qi dynasty, at the age of fourteen, he was invited to Xuande Hall in Jinyang to lecture on the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing).

The Emperor personally presided over the banquet, with both civil and military officials in attendance. The Empress Dowager and the ladies of the six palaces likewise ascended to the Dharma assembly. By imperial decree, the attendants...
Zhonggao Yuanhai ascended the seat with Fu Zong attending him above and below; his divine spirit was firm and lucid, causing the world to marvel at him.

He analyzed principles and opened the way for spiritual insight, such that all followed and revered him. Upon receiving full ordination, he specialized in the Vinaya regulations and advanced in the study of monastic codes.

At that time, Emperor Yang summoned him to the highest rank and ordered him to reside in the inner hall, where he lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* sutras.

In the sutras such as these, however, that which is esteemed in the Eastern Land (China) prioritizes literary prose and verse, whereas the models for teachers in Central India take the Sanskrit sounds (*brahmanī vāc*) as their foundation.
Daocong therefore specialized in seeking out the leaf-scriptures (*pattra-pustaka*), reciting ten thousand words daily.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, *Daśabhūmika*, and other texts were all personally transmitted to him in their Sanskrit sounds; he received, maintained, read, and recited them, examining them in the dark every day until he had mastered them completely.
He ceased [his work]. In the second year of the Daye era, an imperial edict was issued to establish a Translation Hall within the Shanglin Garden in Luoyang to house him.

Altogether, he translated twenty-three scriptures comprising approximately one hundred fascicles. The prefaces composed by imperial decree and the accounts of his life are fully recorded at the beginning of these scriptures.
On the morning of his final illness—the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month in the sixth year of the Daye era—though his physical form was frail...
His spirit was serene. He asked his disciples, "Has the time for the midday meal arrived yet? They replied, "It has not. He closed his eyes and lay down again; this occurred two or three times.
Then he turned his body, extended his neck, and looked toward the door at the sun. "The time for the meal has already arrived; I am now coming to my end.
He sought water to wash his hands, burned incense, and welcomed the painted image of Maitreya. With palms joined, he gazed intently at it, opening and closing his eyes.
After three or four [breaths], as if entering a state of meditative concentration, he suddenly passed away. Only when the silk floss was applied did they realize his breath had ceased.

He was fifty-four years of age; his years since ordination (*śīla-varṣa*) are not recorded. (Regarding "leaf-scriptures" [*yèdiǎn*]: in India, scriptures were written upon *pātra* leaves; hence they are called "leaf-scriptures.")
Dharma Master Huiyun’s surname was Li, and he was a native of Jiangxia.

At the two monasteries of Yuanxing and Longquan, he commissioned one gilded-bronze Maitreya statue for each, with a seated height of one zhang and five chi, in order to establish karmic conditions for his future lives. There was a Magistrate of Wu County...

Chen Shichuo, who had set aside worldly complexities to pursue the righteous path and looked up with devotion to the sound of the Dharma, requested that [the Master] lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras.
As soon as the scrolls were finished, his physical exhaustion and labor increased; he then entrusted his fly-whisk to the scholar Zhizang, saying:

"Study diligently and await questions; do not shrink from the winds of wisdom. If the teacher is at ease while the work is doubled, you need not feel ashamed of being repeatedly illuminated. Once these vows were concluded, he remained serene in silent contemplation.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, Faming passed away at Tongxuan Temple at the age of sixty-seven.
Over a thousand scholars and disciples, weeping with grief and sorrow, together erected a lofty stele for him. (His serene composure at the moment of death was clear evidence of his rebirth;
truly, such was the power of the vows he had made to establish karmic conditions for future lives.)
Dharma Master Xuanzang’s original name was Hui.
His secular surname was Chen, a descendant of Chen Zhonggong of Taichou during the Han dynasty. His grandfather, Kang, was a State University Doctor (Guozibo) of the Northern Qi.

His father, Hui, mastered the classics and arts from an early age. [Xuanzang] stood eight *chi* tall and had clear, prominent features. He served as the Magistrate of Jiangling and was a man of great learning.

He withdrew with his neck-cloth [in place]. His master’s elder brother was Dharma Master Changjie. [The master] daily received instruction in the refined principles and was proficient in the skillful discourses.

At the age of eleven, he could recite the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Lotus Sūtra*. He was preeminent and upright, not conforming to the trends of his time; he recited orally while his eyes remained focused on the objects of contemplation.

He was entirely without negligence or deficiency. At that time, the Dharma assemblies were flourishing in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). Regarding the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Abhidharma* treatises, and other such works, he would not forget anything after hearing them once;

his reputation for this surpassed that of men of antiquity. As he reflected upon the words, he mirrored their underlying principles, such that there was no cave or grotto he did not penetrate to its depths.
At that time, everyone marveled at the power of his memory, which was rarely equaled throughout all ages. When he reached the age of twenty-one, he thought to himself:

In learning, one prizes what endures for the long term; in principle, one values what is comprehensive and penetrating. To delve into and revere only a single aspect is not yet to have plumbed the depths of the mysteries.
Had he not been willing to risk his life and sacrifice his existence, vowing to travel to India, how could he have fully beheld the perfected words? At that time, he was twenty-nine years old.

In the third month of the third year of the Zhenguan era, he traveled westward to seek the sacred traces of the Buddha, proceeding directly to Guzang and gradually reaching Dunhuang, with his route passing through Tian...
He reached the border. Wrapping his provisions and solitary as a shadow, he looked ahead with a sense of vast distance; there was only level sand, utterly devoid of human paths.
Wandering aimlessly, he surrendered himself to fate and pressed on according to his karma. Having endured many perils and hardships, he arrived at Iwǔ and Gāochāng.

The King of Gāochāng provided him with goods and funds, and he was escorted by stages through the Tujue to the various tribes of the Snow Mountains and the Kingdom of Brahmā (Vārāṇasī), where he beheld all five regions of India.

Master Jing traveled through more than one hundred and fifty countries. On the twenty-fourth day of the first month of the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he arrived at the western outskirts of the capital.

Monastics and laypeople alike flocked toward him, gathering in such great numbers that the area was teeming with people; tens of thousands of followers were like those who had encountered the Buddha’s descent into the world.

He was summoned into the inner palace, where he personally attended upon the Emperor’s countenance. Their discussions on the ultimate and conventional truths did not deviate from the Imperial will. From there...

From the hour of the Rabbit (卯) until the hour of the Dog (酉), he did not realize that time had passed so long; he then requested to begin the translation work. The Emperor said, "Since the Master’s departure, I have constructed Hongfu Monastery.
Although it is small, its meditation quarters are secluded and tranquil, making it suitable for translation. I shall provide all necessary personnel, officials, and labor."

He consulted with Xuanling on this matter, ensuring that the requirements were generously provided. An imperial edict further stated: "The officials required to assist in the translation have already been assigned.
As for the stele, I shall compose the text myself; once it is completed, I request that Your Majesty’s divine calligraphy be used to inscribe it. He was granted this special favor.
The day was set for the procession to the temple. Monks from all the capital temples constructed banners and canopies.

Furthermore, by imperial decree, the princes and dukes downward, the officials of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and the Nine Ministries, along with the musicians and performers of the two prefectures, accompanied the cortege in more than a thousand vehicles and halted at Hongfu Temple. The Emperor resided at Anfu Gate, looking down upon the procession from above.
Men and women of the capital lined the sides of the road, stretching from north to south for over twenty li, filling the way.

He traversed the streets and alleys, illuminating the mundane world and promoting the Dharma; there was no one who could equal him. Since my birth, I have constantly harbored the wish to see Maitreya.
Upon traveling to the Western Regions, I further heard that Asaṅga and his brother were both born in that heaven. I repeatedly offered prayers, and all received signs of their fulfillment.
Bearing this in mind with single-minded devotion, my diligence increased all the more. Later, when I arrived at Yuhua Palace, there was no moment of leisure that I did not [devote to this].
He made a vow to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven to behold Maitreya Buddha.

Having personally completed the translation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in six hundred fascicles, he exhorted himself alone to be diligent in practicing the Way, performing prostrations and repentance. In the first year of the Linde era, he addressed the monks engaged in translation and his disciples, saying:
"All conditioned phenomena inevitably return to decay and extinction. How could this bubble-like and illusory physical form endure for long? I am now sixty years of age."
"I am fifteen [years old]. I shall surely pass away at Yuhua. If you have any doubts regarding the sūtras or śāstras, you may now ask quickly.
Those who heard this were startled and said, "Your years are not yet advanced; why do you speak such words? He replied, "I know this myself. Thereupon, he went to take his leave of the Buddha.

First, he fashioned ten billion images of the Buddha, and performed prostrations, repentance, and farewells. He addressed the monks of the monastery, saying, "Xuanzang will surely die. Regarding the sūtras...
He said, "This body is loathsome, just like a dead dog. Once I have died, bury me in a secluded place near the mountain of the palace temple.
Because he was bedridden with illness, as his eyes opened and closed, he saw a great lotus flower, pure white, approaching him.

He also saw the majestic form [of a Buddha] and knew that he would be reborn before the Buddha. After he had ordered the monks to read the titles of the sūtras and śāstras he had translated, there were seventy-three in total.
[The] sections [total] one thousand three hundred and thirty scrolls. From the moment he felt joy within himself, he summoned his disciples;
those with whom he shared a karmic connection gathered together. As impermanence was about to arrive, he urged them to come and see him.

Having bid farewell to the monks of the temple and his disciples, and having completed his final memorial petition, he then silently recited the name of Maitreya and instructed those nearby to chant: "Namo Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. May [I...]"

May all sentient beings quickly behold his compassionate countenance. *Namo* to Maitreya Tathāgata. May those within the inner assembly who reside there, upon the end of their lives, surely be reborn therein.
On the fourth day of the second month, he sat with his right side toward the north, his feet stacked one upon the other, his right hand supporting his head, and his left hand resting upon his thigh;
he remained perfectly still and motionless. When someone asked what sign this was, he replied, "Do not ask; it hinders my right mindfulness. This continued until the fifth...

At noon on that night, his breath ceased and his spirit departed. Two months passed, yet his countenance remained as usual. There were also spiritual responses from the unseen realm, which I shall not describe in detail here.

An imperial decree was issued regarding the date of the funeral, permitting the monks and nuns of the capital to escort the procession with banners and canopies. Thereupon, white canopies and white banners drifted through the air like gathering clouds;
the mournful sound of the *jia* flute and the chanting of the *brahman* priests stifled both the senses and the spirits. The four classes of the laity were moved to grief by this. Seven...

The multitude lamented his profound stillness. The Emperor personally came to the city wall to gaze upon him as he was sent off. By imperial decree, he was interred at the White Flower Plain (Baihuayuan) within a silver inner coffin and a golden outer coffin, identical to those used for the Tathāgata.
Later, by another decree, he was reinterred in Fanchuan and subsequently exhumed once more. All who witnessed this marveled at its wonder.

Although he had been buried for a long time, his physical features remained as they were at the beginning. Were it not for the sustaining power of his vow-force (*praṇidhāna-bala*), how could such a thing have been brought about?
This is recorded in detail in his own biography.
Vinaya Master Daoxuan’s secular surname was Qian;
he was a native of Dantu. His mother dreamed that the moon pierced her womb before she conceived, and she subsequently dreamed of a Brahman monk.

The record states: "That which you carry in your womb is the Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang dynasty. Sengyou was formerly the monk Senghu of Yinyue Temple in Shanxi during the Southern Qi dynasty;
he should follow [your son] into the monastic life to honor and establish the teachings of Śākyamuni. Thus, he remained in the womb for a total of twelve months.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he descended from his mother’s womb. At the age of nine, he was able to compose poetry; at fifteen, he grew weary of worldly life.

He recited and studied various sutras and received formal instruction under Vinaya Master Zhiyun. At sixteen, he shaved his head and applied himself with single-minded diligence and mindfulness, moving the relics to manifest within a precious casket.
He received full ordination from Vinaya Master Zhishou. Having studied the Vinaya, he listened to it only once before intending to practice meditation.

Master Ying rebuked him, saying: "One travels to the distant by starting from the near; one knows the sublime through the subtle. There is a proper time for cultivation and renunciation, and one's vows must first be fulfilled. It is not yet appropriate to abandon the Vinaya.
He was thus compelled to listen to the Vinaya twenty times more before retiring to the mountain forests to cultivate concentration and wisdom, concealing his traces.

While practicing the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* at Zhongnan Mountain, he was visited by a group of dragons who paid their respects. Whether male or female, they transformed themselves into human form and once presented him with a casket of extraordinary flowers;
these resembled jujube blossoms and were as large as elm seeds, yet their fragrance was so intense that it remained vivid for several years.
They also offered rare fruits, whose flavor was sweet and their color pure, unlike anything encountered in the human world. The Emperor issued an edict [to grant him honors].

Master Xuanzang translated [sutras] and composed commentaries, sub-commentaries, and other works totaling more than two hundred and twenty fascicles. His three robes were all made of *ramie*, and his single daily meal consisted only of beans.
When walking, he relied on a staff; when sitting, he did not lean against a bed. Itches and lice accompanied him as he traveled, yet he remained naturally at ease.
He once constructed an altar, upon which a long-eyebrowed monk suddenly appeared and discoursed on the Way; those who recognized him knew it was actually Piṇḍola. Furthermore, there were three...

The Indian monk performed a ritual at the altar and offered this praise: "Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, while the Semblance Dharma has remained in the world, you alone, O Master, have caused the Vinaya to flourish.

At the beginning of the Qianfeng era, a celestial being appeared in a spiritual vision to discuss the characteristics of the Vinaya, stating that the discrepancies and errors within the meanings of the *Śīlaprakaraṇa* (Commentary) were all the fault of the translators and not the Master’s responsibility. He requested that the Master correct these; therefore, [this work] now..."

His writings and compositions were mostly revisions of existing texts. During the Zhenguan era, he once lived in seclusion at Yunshi Mountain in Qinfu, where people saw a celestial youth attending to him on his left and right.
While performing the night-walking practice (yexingdao) at Ximing Monastery, he stumbled on the front steps;
a being supported him, allowing him to walk upon empty air without harm. When he turned to look closely, it was a young man. Xuánqù immediately asked, "Who are you?"
He was there during the middle watch of the night. The youth said, "I am no ordinary man; I am Nanda, the son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North.
For the sake of protecting the Dharma, I have guarded the Venerable Master for a long time. The Master said, "I am a poor practitioner;
there is no need to trouble the Crown Prince. Your majesty possesses sovereign spiritual power, and in the Western Regions there are matters where Buddhist services may be performed."
"Please procure it for me. The Prince said, "I possess a Buddha-tooth relic. Although I have held this treasure for a long time, I would still sacrifice my head or eyes;
how could I dare not offer it? He immediately presented it to Xuan, who maintained and made offerings to it.
Furthermore, outside the courtyard, a deity came to pay his respects and said, "The Vinaya Master shall be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. He offered a bundle of objects, saying, "These are..."
Jiklinxiang (Skt. *Kakubha-gandha*). One hundred days thereafter, he passed away while sitting peacefully. This was on the third day of the tenth month in the second year of the Qianfeng era.
He was seventy-two years of age and had fifty-two years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera-vassa*). His disciples successively interred him in a stone chamber at Tangu Valley.
Emperor Gaozong issued an edict ordering that the true likeness of the Master be reverently adorned and depicted, as a tribute to his spiritual legacy.
The Master’s adherence to the Vinaya was renowned throughout India, and the beauty of his compiled works flowed across the world.

Consequently, when the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra arrived in the Eastern Land for an audience with the Emperor, the Sovereign asked him, "Having traveled from such a great distance, you must be weary; in what direction do you wish to reside?"
At rest, the Tripitaka Master submitted a memorial, saying: "While in India, I often heard that Vinaya Master Xuán of Xīmíng Monastery held the foremost position in upholding the precepts;

I wish to go there to rely upon him. The imperial decree granted his request. In the tenth month of the tenth year of the Xiāntóng era of Emperor Yìzōng, an edict posthumously conferred upon him the title Chéngzhào (Pure Illumination), and his stupa was named Jìngguāng (Pure Light).
Because he had previously resided for a long time at Zhōngnán, he was styled the Nánshān Lǜ (Nanshan Vinaya Master).
This is the school [of Xuanzang].

Dharma Master Kuiji—whose courtesy name was Hongdao and whose surname was Wei Chi—was a native of Chang’an in Jingzhao. During the Sui dynasty, he served as a military commander at the Western Garrison of Daizhou.

This was the foundation of his lineage. His father’s name was Zong; he served as the Left General of the Golden Myriad-Horse Guard, the Prefectural Governor of Songzhou, and the Duke of Kai-guo County in Jiangyou.
Ji’s mother, Lady Pei, dreamed that she swallowed the orb of the moon with her palm; upon waking, she conceived. When the child was born...
He was unlike the other children; as he repeatedly recited and practiced his studies, his spirit was clear and his intellect sharp.

When Master Xuanzang first encountered him on the road, seeing that his eyebrows were elegant and his eyes bright, yet his deportment was somewhat coarse and casual, he remarked, "He is truly of noble lineage; this is no mistake.
He further thought, "If we should meet through the convergence of karmic conditions and he is ordained as my disciple, then my Dharma will have a place to rest. He then recalled his time in India.
Calculating the date of his return journey, he consulted the Nigaṇṭhas, who cast a divination and obtained an extremely auspicious omen. They said, "Master, simply return to the East;
there, you will produce a sage. He then went to the gate of the general and converted him, leading him to leave the household life. The father said, "He is of a coarse and violent nature."
Regarding that superior instruction, Xuanzang said, "This capacity for such a task could not have arisen except in a general, nor would anyone other than I fail to recognize it.
Although his father had already given his consent, Ji also strongly resisted. After being exhorted and encouraged three times, Ji bowed and complied with the command.

When he reached the age of seventeen, he was received by imperial decree as Xuanzang’s disciple to study the languages of the five regions of India; he resolved entanglements and untied knots, mastering the systems with complete clarity through what he heard and saw.

There was none who did not sigh in admiration and submit in reverence. At the age of twenty-five, he responded to an imperial decree to translate scriptures and lectured extensively on both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, composing commentaries totaling approximately one hundred works.
Later, while traveling to Mount Wutai, he stayed overnight at the ancient Fosi Temple in Xihe; there, he dreamed that beneath the mountain—
There were immeasurable people crying out in extreme agony. A celestial youth appeared, holding two scrolls of paper and a brush, which he cast toward them.
At dawn, as he passed through the Xindu Monastery, a light shone for a long time without fading. Investigating it, he found several scrolls emitting light;

upon unrolling them, he discovered the *Maitreya’s Ascent to Heaven Sūtra* (*Mile Shangsheng Jing*). He then recalled his previous dream, realizing that Maitreya must have commanded him to compose a commentary on it.
He merely sought to clarify its underlying principles. As he took up his brush to write, two sets of seven *śarīra* relics fell from the tip of his pen;
they were as large as Chinese *hántáo* (apricot) fruits, red in color, and lovely to behold. Those that subsequently fell in succession were shaped like grains of yellow *liáng* millet.
Daoji converted disciples wherever he went, and those who received his benefit were numerous. He constantly corresponded with veteran translators and frequently visited them.

Master Xuán was frequently visited by various heavenly messengers and attendants who would inform him of miscellaneous affairs. On such days, Xuán would depart; they would only arrive once he had left.
Xuán marveled at their lateness, and they replied: "Just now, a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva was here, accompanied by a great multitude of benevolent spirits.
Our supernatural powers were thus constrained by them. This occurred in the first year of the Yongchun era, the Renwu year.
He manifested illness and, on the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, passed away at the Translation Hall of Ci’en Monastery.
He was fifty-one years of age; his years since ordination (*dharma-vassa*) were not recorded. Daoci was by nature ever courageous and diligent;

he fashioned an image of Maitreya and, before it, recited the Bodhisattva Precepts once every day, vowing to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. To fulfill this aspiration, a miraculous radiance emanated from his entire body, shining brilliantly.

It may be observed that all Buddhist temple icons throughout the world today depict the figure known as the "Commentary Master of One Hundred Volumes" (Bǎiběn Shūzhǔ). Emperor Gāozōng composed a hymn of praise for him, using his posthumous title and name;
thus he was called Dàchéng Jī. Today, those throughout the land refer to him as the Dharma Master Cí'ēn. (In the world there are foolish people...)

Because he slandered the Master as being of the Hīnayāna, when Daoji arrived, the celestial messenger withdrew. As for the "celestial messenger," this refers to a messenger of the General of the Southern Heavenly King. As for the "virtuous deity," it may refer either to a heavenly general or to a *dharmapāla* (Dharma-protecting) spirit king.

That messenger was like a servant or slave; this reflects the relative dignity of their respective deities, not the relative status of the men themselves. To speak of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva is to refer to the messenger as the honorific title for Master Jì; it does not mean that Master Xuán was small while he was called great.

Formerly, when Master Xuán was walking and lost his footing on the steps, Prince Nàzhá of the Northern Heavenly King personally supported him. Later, when he manifested illness for ten months, the Heavenly King attended upon him without ceasing.

How much more so, then, given that Master Xuán and Master Jì were both born in the Inner Court and together realized non-retrogression—how could there be any distinction between "great" and "small"? It is merely that ignorant people perceive things through their own private biases, venerating some sages while neglecting others, thereby bringing calamity and misfortune upon themselves.

Master Fashang, whose secular surname was Liu, was a native of Chaoge. He entered school at the age of five and mastered the chapters in seven days; by the age of eight, he had gained a comprehensive overview of them.
He studied the scriptures and edicts exhaustively to master their principles. At the age of nine, upon reading the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he immediately conceived a sense of world-weariness.

By the time he was twelve, he left the household life under the guidance of Master Zhuchi, who acted as his spiritual mentor. He recited the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Lotus Sūtra*; within barely twenty days, he had mastered both texts.

When he first began lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra*, he responded to and resolved all doubts and challenges, leaving everyone without exception to sigh in admiration and submission. However, because his physical appearance was not handsome, [he was initially overlooked].
The people of the time had a proverb: "If the Black Śrāmaṇera comes, the high seat shall meet with calamity. Later, encountering perilous times, he lacked both food and clothing;
yet he focused his mind entirely on *nirvāṇa*, having no concern for hunger or cold. Thus, he took a single grain of rice with vegetables and wore a single garment supplemented by grass.
As his physical form was nearly exhausted, his spirit advanced daily. Thereupon, he cast off his light...
He received full ordination. Once his wisdom and karmic legacy had become renowned, the assembly all presented their requests;

he then lectured on the *Daśabhūmika*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and other sections of the canon, with the sessions following one another in succession. He composed commentaries and sub-commentaries for all of them. With the offerings and benefits he received, he constructed a mountain monastery.
At the very summit of the mountain, he constructed a hall for Maitreya, adorned with every requisite and exhaustively embellished with magnificence.

He provided the four types of offerings for one hundred and fifty monks. When the Qi dynasty collapsed and the Dharma was suppressed, even these mountain temples were not spared; yet [Hui]shang privately concealed his secular attire and continued his religious studies as usual. He made this vow:
"If, after my life ends, I am permitted to behold Maitreya, and if there remains a remnant of my years, may I witness the flourishing of the Dharma once more. Once again—

He paid homage to the Tathāgata Maitreya. His physical strength was frail and he was slightly ill; a sedan chair was prepared for him. His disciples carried it as they proceeded to Mount Shengsi Temple.

There, he joined his palms, performed three prostrations, and circumambulated the temple three times to the right. He then returned to his mountain retreat, where he recited the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
Upon finishing the scrolls, he passed away at the age of eighty-six, on the eighteenth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Daxiang era of the Zhou dynasty.
Dharma Master Tanyan’s surname was Xiahou, and he was a native of Nanyanzhou. At the time of his birth, his teeth were already fully formed, which the world regarded as extraordinary.
He began his studies at the age of seven; his intelligence and acumen were peerless. At fifteen, he was appointed to the position of Provincial Governor (Zhoudu). Whenever there was a lapse...

He attended the lectures of Shi. At eighteen, he was nominated as a *xiucai* (talented scholar). Upon attending the Dharma assembly of Master Guang, he immediately received the precepts of return (*guijie*).
He abandoned worldly affairs and devoted himself exclusively to the principles of the Buddha. After three years of study, his achievements rivaled those of the predecessors.

At the age of twenty-three, he entered the order under Master Guang and was ordained. His studies were so incessant that he sacrificed both food and rest; consequently, there was no time for formal lectures.

Fei assisted in elucidating the profound principles of the Dharma. On the eighteenth day of the second month in the first year of the Kaihuang era, he suddenly informed his attendants, "The time of my death has arrived.

He then recited the name of Maitreya Buddha until both his voice and breath ceased. At that time, at the hour of noon, the monks standing nearby observed that his countenance remained serene and joyful.
He was seventy-nine years old. From the time of his birth, his extraordinary features had moved and inspired others.
He established himself in upright integrity. Whenever he saw a scripture or an image, he would invariably pay homage and escort them with reverence.

When he encountered those who were poor or humble on the road, he would always feel deep compassion and shed tears. He constantly delighted in listening to the precepts; throughout his life, he lacked two sūtras—*Vimalakīrti* and *Śrīmālādevī*—which he recited once every day.
Before they were finished, he had a dream in which he saw a man in vermilion robes with spiral hair hanging down to his back, attended by two youths, ascending [into the air].
He faced north and ascended into the heights; shortly thereafter, he passed away. At that time, people collectively regarded him as one who had attained the Way of Heaven.
Dharma Master Daopi was a native of the noble quarter in Chang’an. His mother was Lady Xu, who, in seeking a son for herself, constantly recited the name of Avalokiteśvara.
In the "Chapter on the Gate," it is recorded that she suddenly dreamed of a divine light illuminating her body, and from that moment she became pregnant.

When she gave birth, the child was like a celestial youth. At the age of seven, he suddenly abstained from pungent and fatty foods. Whenever he visited a monastery, he was so filled with joy that he would forget to return home.

He then informed his mother and went to Baoshou Monastery to pay respects to Dharma Master Jieneng, whom he revered as his model and guide. At nine years of age, he was proficient in chanting the *Brahma-svara* (Sanskrit) liturgies; at nineteen, [he attained further realization].
Having mastered the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he began to lecture and expound upon it.

At the age of twenty-seven, he met Governor Lou Jiying of Yaozhou, who invited him to reside at the Fuxian Mili Monastery in Luoyang—the very site where Dao’an of the Jin dynasty had previously translated scriptures.
In the third year of the Tianyou era (the Bingyin year), Prince Ji-yin bestowed upon him purple robes, and Emperor Zhuangzong of Later Tang appointed him [to official rank].
The Great Master was named Guangzhi. He applied himself with great diligence and without slackening.

For each character in the *Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, and the *Sūtra on the Rebirth Above*, he performed one prostration. Furthermore, he practiced the twelve ascetic observances (*dhūta*).
The time for alms-round had arrived, and two disciples accompanied him. Furthermore, he had stood in prostration before the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for two years.
On the eighth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Xian-de era (the year of Yimao), he suffered from a slight illness. On the tenth, he instructed his disciples to prepare congee early.
He announced, "Now many Śūraṅgama Bodhisattvas have come to welcome me. He then struck the wooden gong, and immediately after, he passed away.
He was sixty-seven years of age and forty-seven years since his ordination. Śūraṅgama Bodhisattvas are found mostly within the Inner Court;
that they came now to welcome him is clear proof of his rebirth in the higher realms.

to carve jade). Kai (pronounced kǎi; fine iron). Qiúlín (upper character pronounced qiú; lower character pronounced lín; both are beautiful jades). Xuā (pronounced kuā; the flourishing of flowers). Six.

*Shifǎxiǎngdōushuài Guījìng jí*, Scroll Lower. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzàn of Bǎoxiànglín Monastery in Nánhǎi, Guǎngzhōu, while residing at Jíqí. To serve food to one who is honored. *Guījìng jí*:
