The remainder of the Middle Collection:
Master Xi (Xi-fashi).
A native of Beizhou, he was a disciple of Master Sengxiu. He took refuge in the Triple Gem at the age of eighteen and made the recitation of sutras his vocation. Later...
He listened to the sutras, taking the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as his primary tenet. His reputation resounded throughout Guandong, and he was highly regarded by the era’s preeminent scholars.

Following Huishou, he entered the capital, where his duty was to provide instruction and exhortation. He had a disciple named Minghong, who was skilled in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and likewise enjoyed great renown at the time.

He succeeded to the master’s legacy and was summoned to enter Puguang Temple, where he frequently propagated the Dharma; however, he devoted himself specifically to managing the provision of bathing services, washing twice every month.
Sengji followed in the footsteps of Master Dao’an and turned his heart toward Maitreya; thus, at the time of his death, he attained right mindfulness and, as he had vowed, ascended to Tuṣita.
— Chan Master Zhixiao.
Xiao—whose clan and lineage are unknown—gathered a community of Chan practitioners to cultivate themselves and transform the common people, providing for those studying in meditative concentration.

Knowing his end was near, he urgently summoned Master T’ai to give him his final instructions. He ascended to the Buddha Hall to pay his respects and bid farewell, and addressed the entire assembly of monks throughout the monastery, requesting their joy and well-being.
As the great vegetarian feast at Chanju Monastery was about to conclude, he said to T’ai: “I am going to the Tuṣita Heaven to listen to the *Prajñāpāramitā*.”
When [Hui]qu was about to depart, Huitai said, "Brother, you go on ahead; I shall follow in seven days. That night at the third watch, he sat in meditation and passed away.
At the fourth watch, his consciousness traveled to Bianxue Temple, which was ten *li* away. It arrived before the bed of Master Huitai; the light there was as bright as day.
He said, "I wish to travel far, and thus have come to bid you farewell. I cannot remain long. Huitai saw him out through three gates.

Having finished his private conversation outside the gate, he entered the room and sat upon his couch; suddenly, it became dark once more. His disciple asked, "I heard the sound of your voice conversing with someone.
He then took a lamp and shone it all around; the three gates were all closed. Only then did he realize that the divine power of the Master was such that he could enter and exit without obstruction.

He immediately dispatched someone to inquire, and it was confirmed that [Fatai] had already passed away. Seven days after Fatai’s death, [Huiyuan] sat upright and ended his life. His two skull-bones were entirely seamless.

Furthermore, there were meditation masters such as Wu Chun and others who possessed many miraculous powers; they likewise sat in meditation until their deaths, but these instances will not be related here in detail.

Chan Master Zhixi: His surname was Chen, and he was a native of Yingchuan. From his childhood, he was extraordinary among his peers; even as a youth, his mind dwelt beyond the mundane world. Witnessing old age, sickness, and death, he realized the transience and peril of worldly existence.
Vowing to transcend the toils of saṃsāra, he sought out sublime environments. Having heard that the Great Master Zhiyi had resolved to dwell on Mount Tiantai, he went there to take refuge.
At Chanfong, he warned and instructed those on the path of delusion, serving as a guide for the world. With sincere devotion, he yearned for him from afar and traveled across the vast blue waves;
at the age of twenty, he finally fulfilled his aspiration. Once he had met him, they immediately established the relationship of teacher and disciple.

His observance of the Vinaya precepts was perfect, and having received the secret instructions of Chan, he further cultivated meditative concentration with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire. Hearing the sound of the great bronze bell of Dongshan, its profound resonance shook the earth.
Gu said, "Aha! They are calling me. Within a few days of this, he told his disciples, "My life will not last much longer.
Prepare fragrant water for me to bathe and enjoy myself. As for the birds and beasts of the mountains—those of extraordinary colors and strange forms that we do not usually see—"
They all gathered by the side of his room, treading upon the ground and soaring through the air, wailing and calling out in lamentation; they did not disperse until after many days.
On the night of the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Zhenguan era, he sat upright in the full lotus posture, holding a *ruci* (fly-whisk) as he preached the Dharma.
When his discourse on the profound principles was concluded, he said to his disciples, "I have met you all in this fleeting moment; now we must part forever.
There is no appointed time for us to meet again. Having spoken these words, he became silent and motionless.

After a long while, as the disciples were weeping, he opened his eyes and admonished them, saying, "Human life is subject to death, and all things must end after they begin. Such is the nature of the world; why should it be a cause for grief?"
"You may go; do not disturb me. He further said, "Since I began practicing dhyāna until this day, forty-nine years have passed, and my back has never touched a bed.
I have not failed those who provided me with offerings of faith, nor have I failed those who maintained the incense and lamps.
If you wish to meet me, you must diligently exhort yourselves to practice the Way; let your efforts not fail others. A disciple asked, "I do not yet understand, Master..."
"Where shall I be reborn? He replied, "Your retribution lies in Tuṣita. The palace is blue in color; it is located to the northwest of the heavenly realm.

(According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tuṣita Heaven constantly loves the color blue, employing the blue-colored samādhi to destroy the attachments of this heaven. There, I saw the Great Master Zhizhe.
On his left and right were various devas and humans, all seated upon jeweled thrones, yet one throne alone was empty. I asked the reason for this, and he replied, 'After Guanding has passed away...'"
Six years hence, he was destined to ascend this [seat] to preach the Dharma. On the morning of the eighteenth day, he addressed his disciples:
"You must all prepare your midday meal early; my life is at its end. When noon arrived, he sat cross-legged, upright and solemn, his breath becoming faint and subtle.
As if entering meditative absorption, he did not return from that state. At the age of seventy-two, a sound of stringed and wind instruments arose in the void, heard by the entire assembly;
it ceased after a long while. After several days had passed, he was finally placed in a stone niche.

His countenance remained radiant and joyful, and his hands and feet were supple, no different from when he was alive. On the seventh day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, Guanding [recorded this].

The Dharma Master passed away at Guoqing Temple; indeed, the words of Chengxi were not false. (The Biography states: When the Great Master was nearing his end, his disciples asked him, "We do not know where the Master will be reborn after passing away.

He replied, "My teachers and friends have all followed Avalokiteśvara, who has come to welcome me. The *Fuxing* [Commentary] says: "Yet while the Great Master was alive, he constantly aspired to be born in Tuṣita Heaven. That at the time of his death he said Avalokiteśvara had come to welcome him—this should be understood as his guiding others according to their capacities and responding to conditions in establishing his teachings;

it cannot be judged by a single standard. According to the *Amitābha Sūtra*, those of the Middle Grade of Rebirth are personally welcomed by Amitābha and the various great Bodhisattvas; how could it be that only Avalokiteśvara alone would receive the Great Master Zhizhe? Thus we believe this."

It is said that for a Bodhisattva of this rank, it would indeed be better to have no middle-grade [teachings], as these were established according to the capacities of beings. What I, Xi, have observed is precisely the long-cherished vow of the Wise One (the Buddha).
Dharma Master Huixian’s surname was Zhao;
he was a native of Puzhak in Hedong. Although he had extensively studied many works, he focused primarily on the two sections of the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras.

This was the ultimate teaching for the beginning and end of his life. Until his final years, his devotion deepened ever further. He said to others, "These two treasures are like wish-fulfilling jewels;
do not neglect them or abandon them even for a moment. In a dream, a monk told him, "In the coming winter, you shall surely ascend to be born in the Pure Land.
When the ninth month arrived, he felt slightly unwell and realized his end was near. He then addressed his attendants:

He said, "I have been a renunciant for many years and have repeatedly received the Bodhisattva precepts. Now I wish to receive them once more. He summoned the various virtuous ones (mahāsattvas), but none responded to his summons.
They replied, "Virtuous one, you merely discipline yourself; what is called 'delivering others'?

He further said, "Simply take the *Śīla-sūtra* (Precept Text) and, having finished reciting it, rejoice within yourself. Then he ceased his efforts in silence. That night, extraordinary celestial immortals appeared, scattered like stars across the sky.

Before and after [this event], he engaged in lofty discourse and extensive exposition, sometimes concealing himself and sometimes revealing himself, witnessed and heard by the entire monastery. On one occasion, when the sun was approaching noon, he was seen with a Buddha image that had not yet entered his room;
suddenly he rose from his seat, joined his palms, and called to the assembly, saying: "Though the great limit of life is long, the small period is but a single thought-moment.
May you all dwell in well-being; I wish to serve as a cause and condition for the great assembly throughout kalpas. He then lay down and passed away. His age was... [years].
Seventy-fifth. This was the seventeenth day of the eleventh month in the sixth year of the Yonghui era.

The monastery had the Dhyāna Master Heng, who was preeminent among his contemporaries and renowned in the capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang. He practiced the path of Maitreya, vowing to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
Having witnessed signs of spiritual response through his cultivation of the *xiánxíng* (ascetic practices), he was certain to behold the Compassionate One.
Chan Master Facheng’s secular surname was Fan, and he was a native of Wannian in Yongzhou. He left home as a youth and resided at Wangxiao Temple in Lantian, where he served the śramaṇa Senghong.
He took the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as his constant practice. He later visited Xiang Chan at Changelin Temple.

The Master consulted with Dingxing, whose virtue flourished as a model for his contemporaries and whose learning was so eminent that all looked up to him. Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, admiring his virtue, requested that he follow the monastic precepts as a guiding example;

however, the Master submitted a memorial firmly declining. He then traveled far, carrying his book-box on his back, until he had a dream in which Samantabhadra exhorted him to transcribe the Great Teaching.
"The Great Teaching," he said, "is the Mahāyāna—the wisdom of all Buddhas, namely Prajñā. At that time, there was a scholar named Zhang Jing.

At that time, he was renowned as a master calligrapher; few could surpass him. Consequently, [the patron] invited him to his mountain retreat, where he was instructed to observe the *upavāsa* precepts and cultivate himself with purity.
He was to hold fragrant liquid in his mouth and wear fresh garments, remaining serene and focused on his task. With all his might, he transcribed the work.

From the beginning until the end of the volume, he sincerely and constantly burned incense as an offering before his desk. Amidst every stroke and dot, his mind remained focused and his eyes fixed upon the text.
He examined [the texts] with such thoroughness that nothing was omitted. At times, a strange bird appeared, its form and color rare and extraordinary;
it would fly into the room, pacing and dancing about, descending to the desk where the scriptures lay, becoming naturally tame and familiar. After a long while, it would soar close by.

The following year, when the transcription of the scriptures was completed and preparations were being made for their consecration, the bird flew there once more. Instances such as these occurred repeatedly and cannot be fully recounted. This continued until the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era.

At the end of summer, he suddenly fell ill. Knowing that his life was coming to an end, he expressed his wish to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. After requesting water for a bath, he again requested a palanquin;

he personally supervised the arrangements himself and would not permit any display of grandeur or luxury. Toward the end of the month, as the sun was about to rise, he spoke without apparent cause, saying:

"You may enter as you wish; I have no leisure for lute and song at present. He looked toward his attendants and said, "I have heard that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and that birth and death do not abide.
That the nine grades attain rebirth—this saying has been proven true. Now there is a youth to welcome me, who has been waiting outside the gate for a long time."
"I am now departing. You all must not let the Buddha’s true precepts decline, lest you later come to regret it.
Having spoken these words, light issued from his mouth, illuminating the interior of the hall. Furthermore, a wondrous fragrance wafted forth in full abundance.

He was seen sitting upright and solemn; one did not realize that his spirit had already departed. At that time, he was seventy-eight years old. (Since he vowed to be reborn in Tuṣita, why speak of rebirth in the nine grades?)
The sublime realm of Tuṣita appeared before him; this was immediate proof that his rebirth in the nine grades of the Pure Land was not in vain.
Chan Master Deng of the Mahāyāna Lamp was a native of Aizhou. In his youth, he accompanied his parents by sea to the country of Dhavalapattana. It was only then that...
He left the household life and later accompanied the Tang envoy Shan Xu to the capital, where he received full ordination from Dharma Master Xuanzang.

After residing in the capital for several years, longing to pay homage to the sacred traces of the Buddha, he took with him Buddhist statues, sutras, and treatises, and traveled to the Kingdom of Siṃhala to worship the Buddha’s tooth relic.
Having fully exhausted his mastery of spiritual wonders, he traveled east of East India to the country of Tamralipti, where he stayed for twelve years.
There he studied the Sanskrit language and diligently cultivated meritorious deeds. He met the Dharma Master Yijing and followed him to Central India, arriving at Nālandā Monastery.
Next, he traveled toward the kingdom of Vaiśālī and arrived at the city of Kuśinagara. There, he frequently sighed to himself, saying:
"My original intention was to propagate the Dharma, for which I had long set my heart upon the Eastern Land. Yet my resolve has not been fulfilled; alas, my years have suddenly declined.

Although today I do not accord with my original aspiration, I vow that in a future life I shall complete this purpose. He regularly cultivated the practices for rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven and dreamed of meeting Maitreya Bodhisattva. Daily, he would paint [the image].
"One branch of the dragon-flower (nāgapuṣpa), weighing one *liang*, is used to mark the arrival of the mind," and so forth.
Dharma Master Xiyuan’s name was Yuan;

his secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Gusu. Although his kinsmen were powerful and wealthy, he alone renounced the household life and followed [the Master] to receive the precepts. Then...
He traveled among lecture halls, never remaining confined to a single location. Diligently cultivating the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), he expounded upon the sūtras and śāstras.

He subsequently composed several fascicles of the *Xuánzhōng chāo* (Commentary on the Profound), all of which perfectly exhausted both the phrasing and the meaning. He constantly exhorted others to urgently cultivate the practices for rebirth in the [Pure Land] above, saying:

"It is not difficult to know; it is the practice that is difficult. You all must strive in this! He himself maintained the six-period liturgy of repentance throughout his life, never failing in the slightest. He was named Yuán.
In his practice of cultivation, he vowed to behold Maitreya. One day, during a lecture, he sat upright and passed away upon the Dharma seat.

At that time, the assembly smelled a wondrous fragrance wafting through the air, and celestial music resounded with a clanging clarity, sometimes ceasing and sometimes continuing for seven days. Was this not a true sign of rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven?
This occurred in the fourth month of the second year of the Qianning era. His body was cremated, and over seven hundred śarīra relics were collected. [The text ends here.]
A person from Siming brought [the text] to the kingdom of Silla.
Dharma Master Lingyin—
whose surname was Yang and who was a native of Wenxiang in Shanfu— while traveling through Changshui in Luonan, encountered lay devotees whose hearts were turned toward the Dharma.

He constructed a monastery, within which he lectured on the sutras and śāstras for over thirty years. Every day, he would recite the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Sūtra of the Descent from Tuṣita* as his regular practice.
Maintaining his conduct and upholding his mind, he vowed to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. This was in the second year of the Qingtai era, the year of Yiwu (475 CE).
He finally passed away at Yisi Temple at the age of seventy-one, with fifty-one years of *dharma-lakṣa* (seniority).

Upon his cremation, *śarīra* relics were obtained, and the disciples and lay donors jointly erected a stūpa for them. As the *Sūtra on the Descent into the World* states: "If disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha practice the pure life (*brahmacarya*) and come to my presence;

or if they uphold the Dharma and come to my presence; or even if there are those who transcribe sūtras and verses onto silk and offer them—those who perform such offerings shall all come to my presence."
Master Zhenhui’s name was Hui;
his surname was Bao. He was a native of Chushan in Wu Commandery. Throughout his life, he specialized in lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* while also extensively reading the texts of the Great Canon.

He practiced the Way during the two periods of the day, remaining diligent and tireless. As for the various arts and the doctrines of the hundred schools of thought, he set them aside in his scholarly discourse.

Aside from this, he admonished his disciples, saying: "The doctrines of heterodox schools muddle and disturb the true mind; being indeterminate, they leave no seeds for cultivation. Why must one practice such worldly customs?
My sole wish is to let out the lion’s roar, not to make the cry of a jackal.

Let us instead focus exclusively on incense, candles, and the sweeping and cleaning of the temple, cultivating the karma for rebirth in the Pure Land, taking the Inner Court as our place of rest. This continued until the second year of the Qingtai era of the Later Tang dynasty.
On the tenth day of the second month, he summoned more than fifty disciples and personally prepared scented water for a bath.
He ordered them to chant the liturgy for Rebirth Above while worshipping the Buddha, and he completely renounced his clothing and resources as offerings for the Saṃgha outside of the regular season.

On the eleventh day, facing the empty sky, he joined his palms and said, "I laboriously invite the holy assembly; please come forth from the void to welcome me. A full hundred followers were present that day, and all heard the sound of celestial music.
He passed away in an instant. His secular age was seventy-three; as a monk, he had fifty-four years of summer retreats and fifty-four years of ordination seniority.

He calculated that he had lectured on the sutras thirty-seven times and read through the Tripitaka twice. On the eighteenth day of the second month of that year, he was buried at the site of the East Temple Estate in the suburbs of Jun.
A procession of banners and ritual implements accompanied by approximately one thousand disciples, both monastic and lay, attended his funeral.

The Sūtra states: "If there are those who diligently cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues, without failing in their dignified deportment, sweeping the stūpas and smearing the ground with clay, making offerings of various famous incenses and exquisite flowers, and even contemplating the images of the Buddha or invoking the name of Maitreya while making great vows—then at the end of life, in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, they shall immediately attain rebirth upon a lotus flower in Tuṣita Heaven.

Master Zhen was precisely such a person. Ancient sages regarded those of heterodox learning as the howling of jackals; the Sūtras and Śāstras likewise state that studying external texts is like using a knife to cut mud.

It is like gazing at the sun and thereby injuring one's own eyes; even now, people still fear that their learning will not suffice, so how could they not be concerned that their self-injury is not profound enough?
Dharma Master Hengchao’s surname was Feng;
he was a native of Fanyang. His grandfather did not serve in office, and for generations his family had cultivated the Confucian Way. Their household possessed wealth amounting to tens of millions.
From birth he was exceptionally intelligent. Even as a young child, he did not engage in idle play. At the age of fifteen, he had early mastered the Six Classics;

he was particularly adept at reciting the *Sāo* (Elegies), his phrasing and tonal modulation being so novel that they spread through the mouths of the people. One day, while reading Buddhist scriptures, he suddenly attained a clear and profound awakening.
He then sighed, saying: "Human life, with its wealth and honor, is like an illusion or a bubble. Only the True Vehicle can provide transport across the sea of suffering.

He subsequently entered the Zhubi Temple to renounce the world and studied the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. For over twenty years, he lectured on various sūtras and śāstras, delivering more than thirty recitations of each.
His integrity and character were lofty and transcendent; among both the clergy and the laity, there was none who did not feel awestruck and reverent upon seeing him.

At that time, the Prefect, Lord Li, who had long admired his lofty character, wished to submit a memorial to recommend him for the purple robe. When Chao heard of this, he was startled and composed a poem, writing:
"In vain I wear these coarse robes, an old man; Floating in my cup, the Way remains unfulfilled. I vow to transmit the sutras and treatises unto death;
I shall not be stained by profit or fame in life. I weary of trees obscuring the mountain’s hue; I cherish the window facing the moon’s brightness. In days to come, I shall follow Fan [Licheng]."
Lí. With a single oar, he made the Five Lakes clear. Master Lǐ Jūn-rù sent someone to exhort him; Chāo remained firm and unshakable.

When the State Councilor and Prince of Yíng, Fēng Dào, heard of his reputation and learned that he was a kinsman from their own region, he first sent him a letter expressing his intent to seek his guidance.
Chāo said: "I am but a humble man. Having abandoned my parents early on, I have devoted myself to the practice of cultivation. My original aim was to [attain] Mí..."
I, Le, know my name. I did not expect it to be casually transmitted to the ears of a high minister. What benefit would this bring me?

Yet, urged repeatedly by my disciples, I could not help but reply with this letter, setting forth in detail that for one who has left the household life, how could empty fame or meager profit possibly matter?
He remained focused on his practice until the third day of the second month in the second year of the Qianguo era, when after several days of slight illness, he passed away at this monastery.
The entire monastic community heard the sound of celestial music resounding through the air; this was clear evidence that he had ascended to Tuṣita Heaven.
He was seventy-three years of age and had thirty-five years of seniority as a monk (*śrāmaṇera*). Upon cremation, more than two hundred *śarīra* relics were collected and distributed.
Externally, fifty pearls were sealed within a stupa erected at this monastery (those who seek fame and profit, upon reading this biography, should reflect inwardly and take timely heed).
The Mountain Deity of Xunzhou.

During the Tang dynasty, Vinaya Master Xuán asked a celestial deity: "In the northern mountains of Xunzhou in the South Sea, within the borders of Xingning County, there is Lingkan Temple, which possesses many miraculous traces.
Why is this so? The deity replied: "This is because it is for this mountain that the holy Mañjuśrī’s disciple [resides]."
The mountain deity had committed many evil karmas. Mañjuśrī, taking pity on him, came to convert him.

The deity subsequently recognized his past lives and requested that Mañjuśrī leave a trace of his presence so that he might constantly pay homage to it and thereby escape all evils. Mañjuśrī manifested [this image] for him; this is that very one.

In the third year of the Zhenguan era, the mountain deity passed away and was reborn in Tuṣita Heaven (as seen in the *Fuzhu yi*; according to the sutra, "Good sons and good daughters, if they violate various prohibitions and precepts and commit manifold evils...").

Upon hearing the name of this Bodhisattva’s great compassion, one prostrates with the five limbs touching the ground and repents with a sincere heart; thus, these various evil karmas will swiftly become purified. (This is it.)
Dharma Master Jilun:
His secular surname was Cao, and he was a native of Jinyang. He entered the monastic order at a tender age; his discerning wisdom surpassed that of others. After receiving full ordination, he...

By the age of twenty-one, his mastery of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was complete. Its profound and subtle principles, as well as the two treatises on Vijñaptimātratā and Hetuvidyā, he could lecture upon after a single reading.
Consequently, he composed commentaries on them; furthermore, he compiled the three-fascicle *Fahua chao*.

In the tenth month of winter during the Jisi year of the "Pseudo-Han" era, he manifested illness and, with mental aspiration and oral instruction, vowed to be reborn in the Inner Court of Tuṣita. After his passing...
The top of his head became hot and only cooled after half a day; this was the second year of the Baoying era. He reached the age of fifty-one.
After the cremation was completed, śarīras were recovered from the ashes, which were then taken by people from near and far to be offered in worship.
Chan Master Jian, whose secular surname was Zhang, was originally a native of Nanyang. Having reached the prime of his youth, he suddenly developed deep faith in the principles of Buddhism;

he subsequently abandoned his wife and children to seek ordination as a monk. As soon as he ascended to the stage of full precepts, he firmly guarded the "jewel of the mind" and thereby attained realization through *dhyāna*. Suddenly—
Having realized the profound mystery of the Way, Zen practitioners gathered like scales of fish, serving him as filial sons serve their parents. One day, his son came from Guangling to visit him;
he encountered Jian at the temple gate, whose majestic appearance was so stern and solemn that he could no longer be recognized. Thereupon, the son asked:
This was the residence of the Great Virtuous Jian. Jian pointed it out, saying, "It can be found to the southeast. Once his son had departed, he subsequently closed his door and did not go out again;

his severing of the web of attachment was thus like this. In the seventh year of the Xiantong era, the year of Bingxu, in the fifth month of summer, he suddenly went out to visit a donor and took his leave, saying:
"May you cultivate meritorious deeds well. This poor monk shall travel far at the beginning of autumn."

Thus he informed his disciples. On the first day of the seventh month in autumn, having washed his hands and burned incense, and after reciting the name of Maitreya Tathāgata, he lay down on his right side.
That very day, he passed away without illness. He was over eighty years of age. His disciples, following his final instructions, carried his body to the forest to offer it to the birds and beasts.
When they went to look at him again three days later, his flesh and features were as if alive. One—
Having no one nearby, he finally covered it with a cake. After one night, there were traces of foxes and wolves; they had eaten only what was covered, while the body remained as solemn as before.
He then cremated it, collected the remaining ashes, and erected a white stupa over them.

The Bhikṣu Xichen was surnamed Yang and was a native of Bingzhou. When he was twelve years old, he had a dream of a golden man of magnificent and extraordinary appearance who led him into a sacred chamber.
The following morning, he informed his parents and earnestly requested to leave the household life; however, before their permission was granted, he wept without ceasing.
He ate. His parents, pitying his natural disposition and feeling how their hearts were stifled by frustration, finally yielded to him.
He immediately entered the Caotang Monastery to study the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* and the Bodhisattva precepts under a teacher, never sleeping until dawn.

At the age of seventeen, he attended the lecture halls of Vimalakīrti commentaries and gained a rough understanding of its great principles. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination and upheld the monastic rules and regulations. Never...

He was without deficiency. At the age of twenty-three, his mastery of literary meaning and administrative capacity was thorough. He further studied *hetuvidyā* (logic) and *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only), excelling in their exposition.
In the second year of the Tiānyòu era, when the House of Lǐ seized control of Hedōng, Emperor Wǔ invited him to reside at the Jìngtǔ Courtyard of Dà'ān Temple.

There, he provided him with the four requisites of support, while [the Master] devoted himself to studying the Tripiṭaka, cultivating the practices for rebirth in the Pure Land, and establishing a great *asaṃvara* (unrestricted) assembly.

During his fasts, he held five assemblies before and after; throughout his life, he constantly fed himself to wolves and tigers. Entering mountain valleys, wild beasts would sniff at him and then flee.
Furthermore, he would strip naked among the thickets to feed mosquitoes and gadflies as an act of giving.
He subsequently ransomed fish and birds, or provided food for those in prison, or distributed alms to the poor and destitute, or offered banners and canopies at the Jingming Temple. In gold...
He enshrined two stupas. Furthermore, he lectured on the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and transmitted it to the Dharma Master Jìhuī of Chóngfú Temple.

Consequently, for three years he did not leave the gates of the monastery. He performed one prostration for every single character as he recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* once through, and for every character of the *Mahābuddhanāmasaṃgīti Sūtra*, totaling one hundred and twenty fascicles.
In his daily life, he wore only coarse cloth and did not store more than what was necessary for his immediate needs. [The Emperor] of the Jin dynasty... [highly honored him].
The Patriarch was granted purple robes and a posthumous title, which he firmly declined. At Tianzhu Monastery, he manifested a slight illness.

On the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), he chanted the name of the Buddha of the Upper Birth (*Sūryagarbha*) and passed away. He was sixty-three years of age in lay years and forty-four years in monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-varṣa*).
His body was cremated, and several hundred *śarīra* relics were obtained. By imperial decree of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, he was buried on the western mountains by the Jin River. Small.
The stupa exists to this day.

Li Baiyu, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, whose courtesy name was Lètián, was a native of Taiyuan. He possessed an extraordinary intelligence beyond his peers and was skilled in literary composition. At the age of seventeen, he passed the jinshi examination.

He served as high as the Minister of Justice (*xingbu shangshu*) and resided in the Eastern Capital (*Dongdu*). He dredged ponds and planted trees, and constructed a stone pavilion on Mount Xiangshan, styling himself the Layman of Xiangshan (*Xiangshan jushi*).

He once inquired about the essentials of the mind with Master Ning. In the fourth year of the Yuanhe era, by imperial decree, Chan Master Weikuan was summoned to the court to be questioned on the essentials of Chan.
The Emperor commanded Bai Juyi to question the Master, saying: "Since you are called a Chan Master, why..."
He spoke thus on the Dharma. The Master said: "Unsurpassed Bodhi is the Vinaya when applied to the body, the Dharma when spoken from the mouth, and Dhyāna when practiced by the mind.
The Vinaya is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is not separate from Dhyāna.
In the second year of the Changqing era, Yizhi went to Hangzhou to seek the Way from Chan Master Niaoke. Later, he traveled to Mount Lu and again sought the Way from Guizong Chang.

The Zen Master once exhorted one hundred and forty-eight people to form an assembly for rebirth in the upper realm (the Tuṣita Heaven), practicing the recitation of Maitreya’s name and meditating on Maitreya’s countenance, vowing that in a future life they would surely be born in Tuṣita.
In his later years, however, he suffered from wind-stroke and paralysis; he subsequently focused his resolve on the Western Quarter, praying to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
He painted a single scroll depicting the transformation scene of the Western Paradise and made this vow: "The World of Ultimate Bliss..."
The Pure Land is free from all evil realms and manifold sufferings. May those whose bodies, like mine, are afflicted by illness, be reborn together with me in the realm of Amitāyus Buddha.
One evening, while sitting on his meditation couch reciting the Buddha’s name, Yi suddenly passed away.

Yi had previously received the eightfold precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) nine times from Master Ru at Bōtá Temple. (Yi had not yet realized that purity and defilement arise from the mind, and that both suffering and pleasure are illusory; thus, he gave rise to grasping.)

Abandoning worldly attachments, one’s aspirations will no longer be divided. If one awakens to the realization that all is but mind, then even celestial palaces and pure lands are merely transformed realms; they are all, in truth, lands of communal dwelling. Yet, since the four great elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates are not the self, what suffering or joy could there possibly be?
Chan Master Xuānlǎng’s courtesy name was Huìmíng.
He was a native of Dōngyáng in Wùzhōu and belonged to the Fù clan. He was the sixth-generation descendant of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) of Shuanglín.

He entered the monastic order at the age of nine; when his teacher taught him the scriptures, he could master seven sheets of paper per day. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he traveled far to seek out Ānanda Lǜ of Guāngzhōu.
The Master received the full precepts and subsequently studied the Vinaya regulations. He also read widely through the sutras and śāstras.
Hearing that the Tiantai school could clear away the obstructions of the multitude and lead one toward the single principle, he went to Dharma Master Huikai to receive instruction.

Unconcerned with poverty or hardship, he mastered the *Fahua Jingming Da Lun* (The Great Treatise on the Pure Radiance of the Lotus Sutra), the *Zhi Guan* (Stopping and Contemplation), the Chan gates, and all other traces of the teachings of this school. He investigated them thoroughly.

He investigated the ultimate essence. Later, he relied upon Master Sengcong to re-cultivate the methods of contemplation (*guanfa*). He roamed his mind through the Ten Vehicles (*shicheng*) and profoundly merged with the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*).

Through the Fourfold Accommodation (*sixin*), he benefited sentient beings; through the Six Stages (*liuji*), he realized the universal pervasiveness of the essence. Although his mind reached beyond the realm of material things, his body grew weary of the human world.

He renounced his feelings for his fields and homestead, setting his will to dwell among forests and ravines. He lived in seclusion at Zuoxi Rock, taking it as his name. Sitting alone in a single room for over thirty years...

In autumn, he wore garments of hemp and ramie, and sustained himself on coarse vegetables. Every time he knelt with uplifted hands in prayer, he vowed to be reborn in the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven.

While he was concentrating his thoughts, a śarīra suddenly descended from the sky and settled upon the walls of the hall he had constructed. He painted images of Avalokiteśvara and Piṇḍola on the walls;
as he burned incense and focused his mind, a divine light of five colors appeared, witnessed by both monastics and laypeople, who marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
After this, monkeys would come and hold up his alms bowl, or birds would land to listen to the sutras. He taught others without weariness and gave lectures without waiting for a large assembly.
For over forty years he wore a single *uttarāsaṅga*, and for his entire life he never changed his *niṣīdana*.

His food was never of double flavor, and he always dwelt in a humble, one-sided room. He would not burn a single candle unless it was to seek out the scriptures, nor would he do so to visit a holy person.
He did not take a single step beyond his quarters. His meticulous conduct and refined mind were rooted in strict adherence to the Vinaya regulations.

Consequently, śramaṇas from distant regions and elders from neighboring territories flocked to his door until it was blocked. That the teachings of Tiantai flourished so brilliantly—how could this not have been due to these factors?
One day, he looked toward his disciples and said, "My various affairs are now concluded; my years are drawing to a close. [At the time of] the Tiānbǎo...
On the nineteenth day of the ninth month in the thirteenth year, he called to his disciples, saying, "My sixfold realization of the Way is perfected, yet the myriad practices remain unfulfilled.
Precepts are the foundation of the mind; you all must take them as your teacher. He then sat upright and took his final leave. He was eighty-two years of age.
His monastic seniority was sixty-one years. The assembly dreamed that he resided on the fourth story of a jeweled pavilion; this signified the inner court of the fourth heaven.
After his cremation, his relics were divided into two portions: one was enshrined in a stupa on the western plain of Zuoxi, and the other in a stupa on the eastern plain of Dongyang.
Those who practiced his Way called him Zuoxi, and he is regarded as the eighth patriarch of Tiantai.
Dharma Master Faxing was a native of Luojing.

He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and did not associate with worldly customs. He attended to the master’s needs by carrying his handkerchief and fetching water for washing, never shrinking from toil or hardship.

He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Regarding the precepts and monastic protocols, he maintained them without transgression. His integrity was solitary and outstanding;
whatever benefits he bestowed upon others, he did not personally take possession of, but entrusted to his disciples to cultivate merit on his behalf.

He constructed a three-story, seven-bay Great Pavilion for Maitreya, nine zhang and five chi in height, housing seventy-two sacred images of worthies and sages, as well as the eight great dragon kings.
Having completed all the solemn adornments, in the first month of spring in the second year of the Taika era, a voice was heard from the sky saying:
"The time for your parinirvāṇa has arrived; the assembly of Tuṣita Heaven now comes to welcome and escort you. Thereupon, he bathed, burned incense, sat upright, and entered parinirvāṇa.

A stūpa was erected one *li* to the northwest of the temple. (The Sūtra says: The Buddha told Upāli: "In future ages, when sentient beings hear the name of this Bodhisattva’s great compassion, they shall fashion his image...")

[One should offer] images, incense, flowers, robes, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, and perform prostrations with focused mindfulness. When this person’s life is about to end, Maitreya Bodhisattva will emit light from the white tuft between his eyebrows—the mark of a Great Man—and, together with the sons of heaven, rain down *mandārava* flowers to come and welcome this person.

In an instant, this person shall attain rebirth there; meeting Maitreya, they will prostrate with their head at his feet, and before their head has even been raised, they will hear the Dharma and immediately attain non-retrogression on the path to supreme enlightenment. In future ages, they shall meet [the Buddhas].

The Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have declared that this Bodhisattva Maitreya shall serve as a great place of refuge for all sentient beings in future ages. If there are those who take refuge in Bodhisattva Maitreya, you should know that such persons will attain non-retrogression on the path to supreme enlightenment.

When Bodhisattva Maitreya attains Buddhahood, these practitioners shall behold the Buddha’s radiance and immediately receive their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). This is the clear evidence of his arising.
Dharma Master Zhijiang:
His secular surname was Shan, and he was a native of South River, Sanhe County, Youzhou. In the fourth year of the Qianning era of the Tang dynasty, at the age of fifteen, he became a śrāmaṇera.
He then traveled to Liyuan Monastery on Mount Wutai to receive the upasampadā ordination; from that time forth, he carried his staff and traveled.

He requested instruction, selecting his teacher like a bird choosing its perch. His commentaries on the two scriptures, *The Pure Name* (*Vimalakīrti*) and *The Superior Rebirth*, were brilliantly elucidated.

Consequently, he composed the eight-fascicle *Ruiying Chao*. In the first year of the Tongguang era, while residing at the site of the ruins of King Wei, he constructed a monastery; its halls and pavilions were magnificent and worthy of admiration.
Furthermore, he fashioned images of the two venerable ones, Maitreya and Śākyamuni, as well as the sixteen Arhats, all of which were adorned with exquisite colors and craftsmanship.
He emulated the dignified demeanor of a sage. Just as his virtuous affairs were being successfully concluded, he suddenly fell gravely ill.

In the first month of autumn in the fifth year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, he passed away peacefully at the age of seventy-four. At the moment his breath ceased, celestial beings and humans thronged throughout the courtyard as if welcoming a honored guest;
this was a manifest response to his long-standing vow to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. Li Xuan, an Assistant Director of the Ministry of Personnel, composed the inscription for his stupa.

The inscription [states]: "The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* was translated by the Marquis of Anyang. Previous sages have already provided many commentaries and expositions upon it; I shall not preserve them all here now. How regrettable! This priceless jewel is truly not something that those of meager merit can obtain.

Anyang was originally a man of the Juqu people, a younger cousin of Juqu Mengxun. By nature he possessed a powerful memory and had extensively read various books. When Dharma Master Dharmakṣema entered Hexi to propagate and expound the Buddha-dharma, Anyang became resolute in his devotion to the inner scriptures and observed the five precepts.

Regarding the various sutras he read, he was immediately able to recite them from memory; this was his constant pursuit. In his youth, he once crossed the shifting sands and reached the kingdom of Khotan, where he encountered the Indian Dharma Master Buddhasena. He consulted him on the meaning of the Way and its principles. Buddhasena’s natural talent was exceptionally brilliant; he could recite [the entire]..."

He translated one hundred million verses. In the various kingdoms of the West, he was hailed as a "Lion among Men. An Yang received from him the *Secret Essentials for Treating Illnesses* (Chishen biyao zhilibing jing). Returning east to Gaochang, he obtained the *Contemplation Sutra of Avalokiteśvara* and the *Contemplation Sutra of Maitreya*, each in one fascicle. Upon his return to Hexi...

He immediately translated the *Essentials of Dhyāna* (*Chanyao*) and rendered them into the language of Jin. When the usurping Wei dynasty annexed Western Liang, he fled south to Song. He concealed his ambitions and lived in seclusion, refusing to involve himself in worldly affairs. He frequently stayed at pagodas and monasteries, identifying himself as a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*).

Initially, when the two *Sūtras on the Contemplation of Maitreya and Avalokiteśvara* were first produced, Meng Yi, the Governor of Danyang, saw them and praised them highly, treating him with great honor and hospitality. He further requested that he translate the *Dhyāna Sūtra*. As he took up the brush, his hand moved without impediment; in seventeen days, he completed five fascicles.
Because he was free from desire for fame or profit and propagated the True Dharma, both monastics and laypeople alike revered and honored him.
Chan Master Shanben’s secular surname was Dong;
he was a native of Yingchuan. Both his father and grandfather held official posts. His mother prayed before the Buddha, saying: "If I am granted a son..."

He was certainly born with the intent to serve the Buddha. From birth, his skeletal features were exceptionally refined and extraordinary. Upon reaching adulthood, he became widely learned and maintained a life of pure cultivation;

he had no desire for official office and remained silent throughout the day. In the eighth year of the Jiayou era, he underwent the examination for senior monks (*mahābhikṣu*) under the guidance of Vinaya Master Yuancheng.
The Master said to others, "Ben shall one day become famous throughout the realm. He then had him study the *Vinaya* and the wondrous *Lotus Sūtra*.
One night, Ben dreamed of the youth Sudhana, who joined his palms and led him southward. Upon waking, he said, "The holy ones have bestowed their grace upon me;
do they wish for me to travel south to seek out my spiritual friends? At that time, Chan Master Yuanzhao’s reputation was flourishing in the region of Wu, so Ben went there at once.
He went to pay his respects [to the Master]. They reached a silent accord regarding the fundamental tenets. He served him diligently for five years, mastering all its essentials.

Later, while traveling to Fushan, he beheld the magnificent beauty of the cliffs and thickets and formed the resolve to spend the rest of his life there. He subsequently resided at Dajiyan. After some time, he emerged from seclusion to teach at Shuanglin in Wuzhou, in Zhedong;
both monastics and laypeople venerated him, saying that it was as if the Great Being Fu had been reborn. He later moved his residence to Jingyin in Qiantang.

Cizhi succeeded Yuanzhao; his assembly of Chan followers numbered over a thousand. Emperor Shen宗 issued an edict appointing him as the abbot of Fayun Temple in the capital and bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Datong.
Furthermore, following the succession of Yuantong, the gates of the temple were filled with offerings from princes, dukes, and nobles.
His residence consisted of ten thousand rooms, gilded and adorned with azure tiles, appearing like a jeweled monastery springing from the earth.
When he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, he was like an elephant king looking back over his shoulder; many students attained awakening through this.

On the day of Jiazi in the twelfth month of the third year of the Daguan era, he bent three fingers and said to those around him, "There are only three days left. Shortly thereafter, he passed away, and a strange bird circled and cried in the courtyard.
He then departed. On the eve of his passing, several monks from Yue dreamed that the Master was returning to Tuṣita Heaven, saying:
"I shall enshrine my entire body in the upper hall; I am the thirteenth generation under Dajian and the seventh generation under Yunmen."

Dharma Master Zhide, whose courtesy name was Yunyan, was the son of the Liu family of Changliu in Shandong. He left secular life in his childhood and studied the sutras and śāstras until he had fully mastered their profound mysteries.
Emperor Sejong of the Yuan dynasty summoned him for an audience and bestowed upon him a purple robe and a square-cut cassock, appointing him as the abbot of the Tianxi and Jingzhong monasteries.

He lectured daily on the commentaries of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Avataṃsaka*, *Vajracchedikā*, and *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Yogācāra). He was specially bestowed with the title "Master of Buddha Light" (*Foguang Dashi*).
Whenever he conferred the precepts upon the seven classes of disciples, he invariably instructed their parents and brothers to ensure they did not transgress them.

As for the practices of burning incense and branding the forehead, he regarded these as lifelong vows; thus, he constantly used the Vinaya to discipline his own followers. If [the community] were to use common...

Regarding those who resided there, for every single offense they were fined one hundred [coins]; thus, those who committed transgressions were expelled. He lived at Tianxi for over thirty years, wearing but a single robe and a single pair of sandals, never changing them throughout his life.
He did not eat after midday; at night, he sat upright until dawn. Due to the hardship of his recitation, he lost his sight.
Suddenly, he dreamed of a foreign monk who invited him to occupy a high seat within the Inner Courtyard of Tuṣita, while flowers rained down from the sky like a torrent. Because of this—

He manifested a slight illness. On the seventh day of the second month in the second year of the Zhizhi era, he continued reciting sutras without ceasing. After a short while, he took leave of the assembly and passed away while sitting peacefully.
His worldly age was eighty-eight. His coffin remained for twenty-one days; his countenance was ruddy and moist as if alive.
Upon cremation, countless śarīra relics were obtained.
Chengci Ni (Nun Chengci), whose secular name was Jiechu, was a native of Shawan in Panyu, Guangzhou. Her family surname was He. From birth she was exceptionally gifted and unlike other infants;
at the age of five, she refused to eat meat or pungent spices. Her relatives and acquaintances could not keep her within the secular world, so they eventually sent her to a nunnery.
She served the Buddha, enduring toil without weariness, remaining awake for much of the time and sleeping little. As she grew older, her character became firm and steadfast;
she maintained her practice with a disciplined mind, harboring no worldly attachments. She listened to lectures and contemplated their meaning, attaining an insight that surpassed that of others.

In the year Gengchen of the Chongzhen era, at the age of forty-one, she finally received the tonsure and ordination. At that time, because nuns were extremely rare, she had been delayed for many years [in her pursuit of full ordination]. From...
Since receiving full ordination, he specialized in the Vinaya Piṭaka and investigated both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) offenses;

thus, his understanding of what constitutes an infraction and its non-infringement became vividly clear, and his virtuous conduct was as pure as ice and snow. Yet, his spiritual faculties had awakened from a past life, and his aspirations were lofty and transcendent.

He held that benefiting others through the Mahāyāna was his primary concern, deeply loathing all outflows (*āsrava*) and desiring to cast off the constraints of the physical form. He once heard that those born in the lower grade in the Western Land must wait for many kalpas before they can see a Buddha.

None of these were his own aspirations; he desired to be reborn in the world to draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Furthermore, he feared that during the confusion of the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*), even if one obtains a human body, it is easily defiled by greed and anger.
Moreover, in this final age (*kalpa*), spiritual friends are difficult to encounter, and one cannot avoid falling back into lower realms.
One day, while reading the *Tripiṭaka*, he saw that there is rebirth in the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven to personally attend upon Maitreya Bodhisattva for one lifetime.
Even though they had seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, there was no distinction of seniority or precedence among them; thus, they resolved their minds firmly upon the supreme quest.

Consequently, they requested me for a definitive teaching, saying, "May we hear the essential doctrine of the 'Rebirth Above'? I then bestowed upon them one scroll of the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Pure Land*.
He then earnestly requested an exposition of the teachings. I accordingly followed the sutras to demonstrate the essential meaning of the orthodox tradition.

At that time, he practiced contemplation based on the sutras, never ceasing to recite the name with his mind and mouth. Although his physical body was plagued by many ailments, his spirit remained more vigorous than that of others; he had always been fond of sitting in meditation.
Xié rarely sat on a mat. Later, he resided at the Zongchi Hermitage in Guangzhou, where he disciplined his disciples with great severity.
On the full moon day of the fourth month in the *bingxu* year of the Chongzhen era, he announced that he was ill.

On the seventeenth day of the fifth month, at the hour of the horse (noon), while sitting in meditation, he suddenly beheld a Bodhisattva—whose attendant forgot his name—who abruptly led him to the Inner Court of Tuṣita. There he beheld various kinds of adornments.
Majestic and resplendent, the physical marks and signs of Maitreya Bodhisattva were beyond description. He then prostrated his entire body in reverence.
Having finished his prostration, he said: "I pray that the World-Honored One will accept me. The Great Being replied: "Seven days from now, you shall be reborn in this place.
Furthermore, on the twenty-first day, while sitting in meditative stillness, he suddenly beheld Maitreya Bodhisattva appearing before him.
Previously, he had seen himself transformed into the appearance of a youth; he immediately descended from his meditation seat and prostrated, requesting to be taken under [the Buddha’s] care.

On the following day, he said to those who had come to inquire after his illness, "I shall depart tomorrow. You should stay your steps to see me off as I ascend the mountain for cremation," and so forth.
At noon the next day, he called the assembly together and invoked the name of Maitreya Tathāgata, then passed away in silence. At that time...
This was dictated by the nun Jiefang, a fellow student, together with those attending to the sick; I recorded it as it was spoken.

Shi Kaizhi, whose courtesy name was Yuanmu, was the son of the Zheng family of Panyu in Guangzhou. From birth he was exceptionally distinguished; even in his youth, he was already able to write. His calligraphy—

Facheng’s realization was not attained through study or tradition. At the age of twelve, he encountered the mourning for his mother; reciting the "Liao'e" (The Weeds Among Millet) poem, he grieved deeply over her labors, feeling unable to repay even a small portion of her kindness.
Later, reading Buddhist scriptures, he learned of the method for gathering the beans [of liberation], whereupon he reverently observed the precepts as carefully as one protects a goose's pearl.

One day, while reading the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* (Sutra on Entering the Womb), he understood the perils of birth and death and developed a profound weariness with the net of worldly dust. He then petitioned...
His father entered the monastic life. Moved by his son’s firm resolve and courageous spirit, the father rejoiced and followed him.
He further emulated the legacy of the late Prime Minister Pei, personally escorting him with formal letters to the Western Mountain (Xilai Shan) in Yingyi, where Master Shao resided.
At that time, the boy was seventeen years old. Zhang Shu-bu Shanggong, who held these matters in high esteem, thereupon composed [a preface].
His praise is inscribed at the end of these words. At nineteen, he shaved his head and took up service with diligence, never showing the slightest weariness.

In attending to his teacher, he was invariably respectful and cautious; in meditation and recitation, he continued from night until dawn. His innate understanding and literary talent were as clear as water and a mirror.
His gaze was never wandering; he turned his head like an elephant king. His posture when reclining was like that of a lion. He did not speak lightly, nor did he laugh with bared teeth.

Among the multitude, he showed no expression of resentment; toward guests, he maintained a serene countenance. He guided others with patience and kindness, remaining profoundly silent and composed as usual. Truly, he possessed the magnanimous capacity and bearing of a great man;
thus, among both the monastic and lay communities, there were none who did not revere him upon first seeing him. At that time, Minister Hong Tianzhuo beheld him...
He clarified his spirit and attended respectfully by his teacher’s side, filled with boundless admiration, deeming him truly worthy to serve as a model and standard for the Dharma-gate.

As for his posing of questions and challenges regarding the meaning of the teachings, they were beyond the reach of ordinary men; upon hearing them, he immediately grasped the essential intent, and there was no need to inquire further into the principles.

Once, while perusing the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above*, he realized that one could behold Maitreya without leaving the Desire Realm, and attain the stage of non-retrogression without having severed the fetters. Thus, he became keenly determined.
He vowed to seek rebirth in the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven. Having practiced the contemplation for some time, the environment and its inhabitants became vividly clear to him;
Maitreya’s great name was never absent from his mind, whether he was moving or at rest. In the Jichou year of the Daqing era, at the age of twenty-three, he was afflicted by a lingering illness.
Although his body was frail and weak, he never required assistance for rising or sitting. He did not wash his mouth nor partake of food.
Since falling ill, he never once showed a look of displeasure, much less uttered a sound of groaning. Before the Lantern Festival of the following year, he sat in long meditation for half a month.
On the seventeenth day, as medicine was being administered, the Master approached to console him, saying: "The four elements are false and provisional, just like a dream."
"An illusion! You must firmly grasp right mindfulness and not follow the waves of delusion. If emotional thoughts arise suddenly, you will drift and sink into the sea of suffering.
I observe your spiritual state; it will not last beyond this morning or evening. Zhe then smiled and said, "In a world such as this, to depart even one day earlier is to gain one day of peace.
Throughout my life, I have been devoted to the aspiration of personally beholding Maitreya Tathāgata; I believe this to be so."
[The Master] asked, "If it does not go as you wish, how could the sincere words of the Buddhas deceive me?
However, I still wish to recite one scroll of the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* (*Sukhāvatīvyūha*) as my final official document. The Master said, "Do you still remember the text of the sūtra?
He replied, "Certainly, it remains in my breast. The Master said, "Since your physical strength is now diminished, you should maintain pure mindfulness continuously until after you have passed away."
"I shall now take your place and offer it. He then fixed his gaze upward and departed into stillness for eternity.

Upon cremation, his teeth were as white as jade or snow, and his śarīra relics appeared in four colors. Alas! Just as Hui was the gem of the Confucian school, so was my elder brother the jewel of our Dharma gate.
Now that he has suddenly passed away, it is not merely that I have lost my source of nourishment; truly, the Dharma gate has suffered a crushing blow.
The roof beam has collapsed. How lamentable! Recorded respectfully by his fellow student Kai-xing.
Kai-luo was a śramaṇera;

his style name was Tie-you. His secular surname was Li, and he was a native of Fengjian in Shunde County, Guangzhou. Filial piety and fraternal duty were innate in him, and he was kind and compassionate.
At the age of sixteen, Su-rong reflected to himself: "I am submerged in the turbid waters of the sea of suffering;

if I do not wake up with fierce resolve and turn back, there will never be a day when I transcend to the other shore. He then paid homage to his preceptor, Master Zai of Mount Dinghu, and received the full precepts.

After the summer retreat had passed, his spiritual faculties sprang forth with rapidity, like a fragrant elephant breaking its chains. Although his parents wished to detain him, they could not hold him back;

he went straight before the Upādhyāya and requested to become a *śrāmaṇera* in accordance with the Dharma. He served his teacher with pure sincerity and diligence, and his studies were even more assiduous.

Even when reprimanded by his teacher, he never showed the slightest look of displeasure. His deportment and dignified bearing were such that he appeared like a bhikṣu who had long practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
He had always admired his fellow student, Master Zhe, regarding the signs of rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven. With single-minded resolve, he maintained the great name of Maitreya.
In the year Dingyou of the Shunzhi era, he lay ill for seventeen days; though his condition was grave and critical, he did not cease to recite the name with his mind and mouth.
Onlookers marveled that even at such a young age, he could maintain such right mindfulness. This continued until the moment of his passing.
Although his lips and teeth could no longer move, the sound of his recitation of the Buddha’s name remained clear. When his breath finally ceased, his countenance still appeared alive.
From the time he lay ill until his cremation, there was not the slightest odor of decay. From this evidence, it is certain that he attained rebirth in the higher realms without doubt.
This record was compiled by his fellow disciple Kai-xiong.
The Upāsikā of the Zou family, the Upāsikā of Guangzhou, was the daughter of Ke Yu Gong, the Magistrate of Jianyang, and the wife of Kuang Guoxue of Nanhai.
From birth she was intelligent; even in her youth, she followed her parents in observing the fasts and turned her heart toward the Triple Gem. She understood...

There was a Dharma-gate for rebirth in Tuṣita; she consequently called to mind the Honored Buddha Maitreya. Abiding by the teachings within her household, she practiced filial piety, compassion, diligence, and frugality.
She relieved the urgent and pitied the distressed, and took joy in making offerings to monks and nuns. She established a vihāra where the four requisites were never lacking.

Whatever vows or offerings she made, she invariably dedicated them toward rebirth above. Her young sons and grown daughters all renounced their worldly ties to follow her into the Way, without the slightest trace of deluded attachment.

At that time, as the country was undergoing upheaval and turmoil, she could not perform religious rites; she simply recited the Buddha’s name silently in her heart. Consequently, the entire family, both old and young, remained safe and at peace.
She once dreamed of ascending to Tuṣita Heaven and touring its inner precincts. Whenever she practiced repentance rituals, she invariably experienced auspicious omens.
Once, at noon on a day when the sky was bright and clear, a servant boy and a maidservant suddenly saw a person over ten feet tall.
Wearing a tall cap and elegant robes, he entered through a crack in the door and walked slowly across the central hall until he reached his chamber; suddenly, he vanished.
When someone informed him of this, Zou Tianran sighed and said, "All who have life suffer; meeting must inevitably end in parting.

Since my long-cherished vow has been fulfilled, it is time for me to depart. Consequently, he developed a slight illness, maintained a continuous stream of pure mindfulness, and invited a gathering of pure monks.
He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily as an aid for his rebirth. Knowing that the time had come, he requested fragrant water for bathing.

Surrounded by monastics and laypeople, they all together invoked the great name of Maitreya. He then sat in the full lotus posture with eyes closed. When midday arrived, he remained silent and did not pass away.
At that moment, a wondrous fragrance filled the room, and auspicious light shone through the groves. All who beheld it could not help but exclaim in wonder.
This is indeed clear evidence of her rebirth in the higher realms; she was a true hero among women.
This occurred in the third month of the Gui-si year of the Shunzhi era. She lived to the age of forty-one.
Postscript: Sūtra, Dhāraṇī, and Vow Texts Those who wish to advance in the cultivation of sublime deeds must rely upon the holy teachings as their guiding compass.

Extraordinary achievements that transcend the world cannot, by any means, be attained through mere intellectual speculation or subjective insight. Therefore, when practice and principle do not diverge, they correspond to one another just as the eyes and feet work in concert.
Merit and wisdom must proceed together, like the mutual necessity of sails and a rudder. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"One cannot attain birth in that land through meager roots of goodness or causes and conditions of merit. It further states:

"If there are those who are diligent in cultivating various meritorious virtues—sweeping the stupas, smearing the ground with mud, practicing various samādhis, reciting the sūtras, and making great vows—they shall immediately attain rebirth in Tuṣita."
[I] place myself before the Buddha. However, in this present age of the final dharma, people compete in superficiality and neglect virtuous conduct, seeking instead only empty principles.

Their practice and speech thus contradict one another, yet they boast of being equal to the ancient sages. When encountering those who engage in cultivation and upholding the precepts, they slander them as being attached to forms and conceptualizing with their intellectual emotions, falsely claiming to have reached the profound realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
How can they know that the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings—whether manifest or esoteric—is according to the capacities of beings? Or...

Whether gradual or sudden, the skillful application of means is manifold. Sometimes a single principle is manifested through myriad practices; sometimes myriad practices are perfected within a single principle. This is what is meant by:
